_about: Reviewed corrections applied by the app on top of Cliopatria (state borders) and historical-basemaps (peoples layer). Each entry cites the specialist log in content/factcheck/ that found it. Operations on a Cliopatria realm (matched by its row name): clip [from,to] hides it outside those years; hide [[from,to],...] hides it inside them; relabel [{from,to,name,key,addTo?}] renames it in those years (key = colour/selection group; addTo = realms whose area timelines absorb the moved area); note = text shown on the realm; scholarly = peak-area estimate shown beside the map's. Base-layer operations by snapshot year: hide [names] turns a polygon into unrecorded land; rename {old: new}.

Ptolemaic Kingdom.note: Polygons dated 331–324 BCE, before Ptolemy took Egypt, are Alexander's conquests mislabelled in the data; they are shown as the Macedonian Empire. The Ptolemaic kingdom proper dates from 305 BCE. Ptolemy lost Cyprus to Demetrius in 306 BCE and retook it in 295 BCE. His holdings in Cilicia and Lycia were coastal: inland Commagene and upper Mesopotamia were never Ptolemaic and are left out for 307–265 BCE. In 31 BCE the map drew all of Mark Antony's eastern provinces as Ptolemaic. Only Cleopatra's kingdom (Egypt, Cyprus, Cyrenaica and parts of Crete and the Levant coast) is kept for that year. Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE and is shown as Roman from 29 BCE.

Almohad Caliphate.note: The 1260–1343 polygon is the Marinid sultanate (the Almohads fell in 1269) and is shown under that name. The last Almohad army left al-Andalus in October 1228, which ended Almohad rule in Spain; from 1229 the caliphate is drawn only south of the Strait of Gibraltar.

Mamluk Sultanate.note: The 1241–49 polygon duplicated Ayyubid Egypt and is hidden; the Mamluk sultanate begins in 1250. The Ottomans conquered Mamluk Syria in 1516 and Egypt in January 1517, ending the sultanate; the Mamluk expedition to Yemen held only parts of the coast. In the 1250s Damascus and Aleppo still belonged to the Ayyubid an-Nasir Yusuf (the Mamluks took Syria only after Ain Jalut in September 1260), so in 1250–1259 the sultanate is drawn without Syria and the Hejaz. The Ottomans took Syria in 1516 and Cairo in January 1517; in 1517–1518 the former Mamluk lands are shown as Ottoman.

Golden Horde.note: The Golden Horde ended in 1502; The map also starts it only in 1294 (it existed from the 1240s as part of the Mongol Empire). Tokhtamysh raided Azerbaijan and sacked Tabriz in 1385 but did not hold it; south of Derbent, Shirvan was ruled by its own Shirvanshahs, vassals of Timur from 1386. The polygons dated 1547–1695 under this name lie over Mongolia, not the Volga: they are the Mongol khanates (the Khalkha in the north and centre, the Oirats in the west), shown under that name; the Khalkha became Qing vassals in 1691. Western Georgia was never Horde territory and is left out. Tokhtamysh only raided Azerbaijan in 1385, and Timur destroyed Urgench in 1388, so Transcaucasia (1385–94) and Khwarezm (from 1389) are left out.

sources.title: Shirvanshah (Wikipedia): Ibrahim I (r. 1382-1417), founder of the Darbandid line, was a vassal of Timur
Golden Horde (Wikipedia): Timur invaded Khwarezm and destroyed Urgench; the Great Horde ended in 1502
Northern Yuan (Wikipedia): Mongol regime 1368–1635; Oirats united in the west c. 1600–1620; Khalkhas in Outer Mongolia

Inca Empire.note: The Inca Empire fell to Spain in 1532–33. The large 1534–39 polygon is hidden; the remnant is shown as the Neo-Inca State of Vilcabamba (to 1572). The map also under-draws the empire before 1497.

Khmer Empire.note: The Angkorian empire ended c. 1431; later polygons are shown as the post-Angkor Kingdom of Cambodia.

Ngô Dynasty.note: The Ngô ruled 939–965 only; from 966 this polygon is Đại Việt under the Đinh, Early Lê, Lý, Trần and Hồ dynasties.

Sultanate of Malacca.note: Malacca fell to Portugal in 1511; later polygons under its name are its successor, Johor. At its height (15th century) Malacca ruled much of the Malay Peninsula, the Riau Islands and part of eastern Sumatra, but the map draws only a small area at the southern tip and does not reach Malacca town itself. Pieces in central Java and northern Sumatra that the map once gave to Malacca's successor Johor were never Johor's and are removed.

Natalia Republic.note: The Boer Natalia Republic was annexed by Britain in 1843; afterwards this polygon is the British Colony of Natal.

People's Republic of Zanzibar.note: In the 1800s this was the Sultanate of Zanzibar; the 'People's Republic' name dates from 1964.

Yuan Dynasty.note: Yuan rule in China ended in 1368; the remnant on the steppe is the Northern Yuan. The map starts the Yuan in 1294 (proclaimed 1271), and draws it larger than scholarly estimates.

Han Dynasty.note: The Han fell in 220 CE; later polygons are hidden. The map draws its peak smaller than scholarly estimates. From 196 the Han emperor lived at Xuchang under Cao Cao's control, so in the last years the red 'Han' area is land held by other warlords who still recognised the Han, such as Liu Bei in Sichuan. Liu Bei proclaimed himself Han emperor at Chengdu in 221; that outline (cut to Sichuan, Hanzhong and Yunnan) is shown as Shu Han for 221-223. Goguryeo's capital Gungnae (Ji'an) lay outside Han rule, so from 30 CE the Han is drawn west of 126°E (keeping Lelang at Pyongyang). In 40-42 CE the Trưng sisters' rising held Jiaozhi and the commanderies to its south, so Han is drawn north of 21.8°N in those years; Ma Yuan restored Han rule in 43, but the map has no Han outline in northern Vietnam for 44-50.

Sui Dynasty.note: The Sui fell in 618; later polygons are hidden.

Tibetan Empire.note: The Tibetan Empire collapsed in 842; later polygons are hidden. Tibet took the Hexi Corridor in stages after 763 (Dunhuang only in the 770s or 780s), and the Tang garrisons in the Tarim held out until about 790. The map's outline takes all of them in 757, so it is drawn only south of 37°N for 757-763 and south of 39.9°N for 764-785. The Uyghurs took Gaochang (Turfan) in 803, so the Turfan basin and Beiting are cut out of the Tibetan outline from 803.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Protectorate General to Pacify the West

Goguryeo.note: Goguryeo fell to Silla and Tang in 668; later polygons are hidden.

Shang Dynasty.note: The Shang fell to the Zhou c. 1046 BCE; later polygons are hidden. The map shows only the Shang core, far smaller than its sphere of influence.

Hunnic Empire.note: The Hunnic Empire broke up after Attila's death and was gone by 469; later polygons are hidden. Scholarly estimates of its peak are about twice the map's. Attila's invasions of Gaul (451) and Italy (452) were campaigns followed by retreat, not conquests; the map no longer draws them as Hunnic territory.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains

Parthian Empire.note: The Parthian Empire fell to the Sasanians in 224 CE; Ardashir I killed the last Parthian king, Artabanus IV, in 224 CE and was crowned at Ctesiphon about 226. From 225 the former Parthian lands are shown as Sasanian.

Saadi Sultanate.note: The Saadi dynasty ended in 1659; later polygons are hidden (the Alaouites took Morocco in the 1660s).

Sur Empire.note: The Sur Empire fell to the Mughals in 1556–57; later polygons are hidden.

Gran Colombia.note: Gran Colombia dissolved in 1830–31; later polygons are hidden. The southern block is Upper Peru, still held by royalists under Olañeta in 1824, which became the Republic of Bolivia in August 1825; it was never part of Gran Colombia. The Upper Peru block is not drawn after 1823. Venezuela and Ecuador broke away in 1830 and the union was formally dissolved in November 1831, so for 1830–31 the shape is labelled as the three successor states.

sources.title: Bolivian War of Independence (Wikipedia): royalists under Olañeta held Upper Peru after Ayacucho; independence declared 6 August 1825; Bolívar wanted Charcas to join Peru

Greek City-States.note: Greece came under Roman control in 146 BCE; later polygons are hidden.

Sasanian Empire.note: The map ends the Sasanian Empire in 643; it fell with Yazdegerd III's death in 651. Khosrow I sacked Antioch in 540 and withdrew for a Roman payment; Syria stayed Roman, so the map no longer draws a Persian wedge to the Mediterranean in 540–545.

Tang Dynasty.note: The map starts the Tang in 623 (founded 618) and draws it larger than scholarly estimates. The Tang ended in 907; the map leaves 908-910 empty rather than show a united Tang. In 658-665 the map stretched the Tang to the Aral Sea; Sogdiana and the western steppe were loose 'jimi' prefectures under local rulers, so the empire is drawn east of 71°E in those years. Its 661-665 peak (8.7 million km²) also counts the Mongolian protectorates, well above Taagepera's 5.4 million km² (715). Turfan (Xizhou) was a Tang prefecture from 640 to about 790, and the Tarim garrisons held out until about 790, longer than the map shows.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Protectorate General to Pacify the West
Wikimedia Commons: The T'ang Dynasty 618-906 AD, boundaries of 700 AD (A. Herrmann, Atlas of China)

Ming Dynasty.note: The map starts the Ming in 1375; it was proclaimed in 1368. Zhu Yuanzhang held Nanjing from 1356 and proclaimed the Ming there in 1368, but the map shows the Yuan (from 1369 the Northern Yuan) at Nanjing until 1374. Manchuria beyond Liaodong came under the Ming only after Naghachu surrendered in 1387, and the Later Jin took Fushun (1618) and Liaoyang and Shenyang (1621); the outline is cut to match. The Liaoxi corridor (Jinzhou, Ningyuan, Shanhaiguan) stayed Ming until 1642-44; it is cut out of the Qing outline until then, but the Ming outline does not cover it, so it is blank. The long arms to the lower Amur (the Nurgan command, 1409-35) and towards Hami were loose garrisons and tributary peoples rather than provinces.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transition from Ming to Qing

Qing Dynasty.note: The map starts the Qing in 1645; it was proclaimed in 1636 (1619–44 is drawn as the Later Jin). The map's peak is below scholarly estimates. Nanjing and the lower Yangtze, taken by the Qing in 1645, are missing from the Qing outline until the mid-1650s. The Qing army held Thăng Long (Hanoi) only from late 1788 until it was routed by Nguyễn Huệ in early 1789, so the Red River delta is cut out of the Qing outline for 1789-90. Tibet was a Qing protectorate from 1720, with imperial residents (ambans) in Lhasa, but the map draws it as a separate state until 1793.

Mongol Empire.note: The map's peak exceeds scholarly estimates of the empire's extent. From 1260 the empire was split into four khanates (the Yuan, the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate and the Ilkhanate); the map draws them as one realm until 1294. It also keeps Syria Mongol after 1260, though the Mamluks retook Damascus and Aleppo within weeks of Ain Jalut (3 September 1260). After the Mamluk victory at Ain Jalut (1260) Syria is not shown as Mongol; the Mongols briefly took Damascus again only in 1299–1300.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Division of the Mongol Empire

Ilkhanate.note: The map starts the Ilkhanate in 1294; it was founded in 1256 (earlier it is drawn inside the Mongol Empire).

Chagatai Khanate.note: The map starts the Chagatai Khanate in 1294; it existed from the 1220s (earlier it is drawn inside the Mongol Empire). From 1347 the khanate's eastern half became independent as Moghulistan (the Eastern Chagatai Khanate), centred on the Ili region. From 1352 this shape no longer includes Transoxiana, so it is shown as Moghulistan.

sources.title: Moghulistan (Wikipedia): independent from 1347 under Tughlugh Timur; also called the Eastern Chagatai Khanate

Xiongnu.note: Scholarly estimates of the Xiongnu peak are much larger than the map's. Han armies took the Ordos in 127 BCE and the Hexi Corridor in 121 BCE; the map cuts the Ordos out of the Xiongnu from 127 BCE and from 121 BCE draws them only north of about 41°N (the Yinshan line). Ji (Beijing), the capital of the kingdom of Yan, is also cut out of the Xiongnu outline for 208-204 BCE. Scholarly estimates of the Xiongnu peak (about 9 million km² in 176 BCE, Taagepera) include the steppe and Tarim states they dominated, which the map leaves blank.

Seleucid Empire.note: The map's peak is below scholarly estimates. The Seleucid era begins with Seleucus's return to Babylon in 311 BCE, but the map draws the kingdom only from 307 BCE. Antiochus IV invaded Egypt in 170–168 BCE but never took Alexandria, and he withdrew in 168 BCE, so Egypt is not shown as Seleucid. Media fell to Mithridates I of Parthia in 148/147 BCE and Babylonia in 141 BCE. Antiochus VII's brief recovery (130–129 BCE) is not drawn. Tigranes of Armenia ruled Syria from 83 BCE, and Lucullus restored a rump kingdom in 69 BCE.

Abbasid Caliphate.note: The map's peak is below scholarly estimates. Baghdad surrendered to the Mongols on 10 February 1258 and the caliph was executed ten days later; from 1258 Iraq is drawn as Mongol. From 1157 the caliphs again ruled Iraq themselves, which the map still shows as Seljuk until 1194.

Ottoman Empire.note: The map's peak (1595) is below the scholarly estimate for 1683. The map wrongly shows Constantinople as Ottoman in 1402–1406 (it stayed Byzantine until 1453), leaves Egypt and Syria blank in 1517–1518 although the Ottomans conquered them in 1516–1517, and redraws Shah Abbas's reconquest of Tabriz, Yerevan and Shirvan (1603–1607) about five years late. Shah Abbas retook Tabriz in 1603 and Ottoman-held Azerbaijan by 1607 (confirmed by the 1612 treaty), so Iranian Azerbaijan is not shown as Ottoman then.

Kievan Rus'.note: The map's extent is below scholarly estimates.

Maratha Empire.note: The map has no Maratha polygon for 1691–1717 and draws its 18th-century sphere far smaller than Schwartzberg (pl. VII.A) and Turchin. The map has no Maratha state for 1691-1717 and Shivaji's capital Raigad lies outside the small Maratha outline of 1677-90; Raigad, Pune and Satara are cut out of the Mughal outline while the Marathas held them (1674-88, 1708-29), so they show blank. Rajaram's capital Gingee (1689-98) is also missing. The empire ended with the Third Anglo-Maratha War in 1818: 1819 is hidden, and the remaining outline of 1820-45 is Scindia's Gwalior State.

(Delhi Sultanate).note: Scholars differ on the peak: Taagepera and Turchin put it in 1312 under Alauddin Khalji; Schwartzberg (pl. V) and this map show the widest extent under Muhammad bin Tughluq in the 1330s. By 1318 the Sultanate governed Devagiri in the northern Deccan, and the Kakatiyas of Warangal and kingdoms farther south paid it tribute; this map shows only the northern core.

Khalji Dynasty.note: Taagepera and Turchin estimate c. 3.2M km² for 1312, far more than drawn here; Schwartzberg (pl. V) shows the Khalji sphere reaching the far south only through tributary raids. Bengal was not under Khalji rule: Shamsuddin Firuz Shah ruled it as an independent sultan from 1301 to 1322. Devagiri in the Deccan was taken in 1307 and annexed in 1318, and Warangal and Dvarasamudra paid tribute. Bengal (Lakhnauti) was ruled independently by Balban's descendants until Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq took it in 1324, so the Khalji outline is drawn west of 87°E.

British Raj.note: The map keeps Burma inside the Raj after its separation in 1937 (except 1943–44), and has no Raj polygon before 1859 (Crown rule began 1858).

Vijayanagara Empire.note: The map ends Vijayanagara in 1571; its Aravidu kings ruled on until 1646. Until 1378 Madurai and the far south were ruled by the Madurai Sultanate, which Kumara Kampana of Vijayanagara conquered; the map's earlier outline over the far south is not drawn.

Chola Empire.note: The map ends the Chola in 1259 (dynasty ended 1279). No scholarly peak-area estimate exists; the map's c. 0.5M km² is smaller than older estimates. Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur c. 848 and made it the Chola capital, but the map leaves the city in the Pandya kingdom until about 930. Rajaraja I took northern Sri Lanka and Anuradhapura in 993, earlier than the map shows, and after the battle of Takkolam (949) the Rashtrakutas held Kanchi and the north of the Chola country for about twenty years.

People's Republic of Bangladesh.note: The map starts Bangladesh in 1973; it became independent in 1971.

Republic of China.note: After 1950 the map shows c. 81,000 km², about twice the area of Taiwan and its islands (c. 36,000 km²). Until Japan surrendered in August-September 1945 much of eastern China and Manchuria was under Japanese occupation; afterwards the Republic took back those regions and Taiwan (25 October 1945), while Tibet remained de facto independent. Hainan fell to the People's Republic in April-May 1950 (and the Zhoushan islands soon after), so from 1950 the Republic of China is shown only on Taiwan, Penghu and the islands off Fujian.

sources.title: Retrocession Day (Wikipedia): ROC took control of Taiwan on 25 October 1945
Battle of Hainan Island (Wikipedia): 16 April-1 May 1950, PRC captures Hainan
Proclamation of the People's Republic of China (Wikipedia): 1 Oct 1949 in Beijing; ROC retreated to Taiwan by Dec 1949

Kingdom of Kongo.note: The map draws Kongo only for 1440–1669; the kingdom lasted from c. 1390 to 1914.

Empire of Kanem.note: Drawn far too small and starting too late; Kanem is attested from 872.

Chámpa.note: The map ends Champa in 1652; it survived as a Vietnamese vassal until 1832. Champa ceded the districts of Ô and Lý (around Huế) to Đại Việt in 1306, and lost its capital Vijaya and its northern lands in 1471.

Srivijaya.note: Srivijaya's end date is debated (11th–14th century).

Canada.note: The map starts Canada in 1932; Confederation was in 1867 (earlier Canada is drawn within the British Empire).

South Africa.note: The map starts South Africa in 1932; the Union of South Africa was formed in 1910.

Commonwealth of Australia.note: The map starts Australia in 1905; federation was in 1901.

New Zealand.note: The map starts New Zealand in 1948; it was a British colony from 1840 and a dominion from 1907.

Kingdom of Hungary.note: The map ends the Kingdom of Hungary in 1546; under the Habsburgs it continued until 1918.

Xianbei.note: Tanshihuai unified the Xianbei c. 156 and his confederation reached from the Wusun in the west to the Buyeo in the east, but it splintered after his death in 181; Kebineng's later revival (c. 207–235) was centred near the Great Wall. The data's polygon also runs north into Dingling lands south of Lake Baikal, a people Tanshihuai pushed back rather than ruled. For 182–223 the Xianbei are shown as tribes rather than a state.

scholarly.source: List of largest empires (Wikipedia), citing an Oxford reference

sources.title: Wikimedia Commons: Xianbei Confederation c. 160 AD (Zangxuangao, CC0)

Xianbei.log: Reader report: map vs Commons reference map, 2026-11-09

(British Empire).note: Australia was a self-governing Dominion of the British Empire from 1901; it is drawn here as a separate country, but in 1921 it belonged to the Empire just as Canada and South Africa did.

sources.title: Dominion (Wikipedia): 'The Commonwealth of Australia was recognised as a Dominion in 1901'

(French Fourth Republic).note: In 1945 Japan had ended French rule in Indochina (March) and France was only beginning to retake it (from September); from 1946 Indochina, like the Moroccan and Tunisian protectorates, belonged to the French Union until 1954-56.

sources.title: French Indochina (Wikipedia): Japanese coup of 9 March 1945, French reconquest of Cochinchina from 23 September 1945, Associated States of the French Union 1949-54

United States of America.note: Greenland and Iceland were never US territory: US forces were stationed there under 1941 defence agreements while Denmark was occupied, and the shaded part of Germany is the American occupation zone from 1945. Occupation zones and wartime bases abroad are not shaded after they ended: Japan's occupation ended in 1952, US troops left South Vietnam in 1973 and Iraq regained sovereignty in 2004, while Okinawa stayed under US rule until 1972. South Korea and West Germany had their own governments from 1948–49, but the map still shades them as American until 1972; Greenland and Iceland still appear in 1941 and 1945 only because those years' shape also holds the Philippines.

sources.title: Greenland in World War II (Wikipedia): 1941 Kauffmann-Hull agreement allowed US troops; Greenland remained Danish and returned to direct Copenhagen rule after the war
Wikipedia: United States Civil Administration of the Ryukyu Islands
Wikipedia: Japanese occupation of the Philippines

(Vichy France).note: Vichy governed from the unoccupied south of France and ostensibly administered all of France except Alsace-Lorraine; after November 1942 Germany occupied the whole country, and most colonies drawn here had already gone over to Free France.

sources.title: Vichy France (Wikipedia): Vichy 'ostensibly' administered all of France except Alsace-Lorraine; after Operation Torch Germany occupied the whole country

British Africa.note: Nigeria and the Gold Coast were British colonies in 1914 (Nigeria was amalgamated into a single colony and protectorate on 1 January 1914) but are drawn here as separate states. Sudan is not shown as British while the Mahdist state held it (1885–1898), nor Libya after its independence in December 1951.

sources.title: Colonial Nigeria (Wikipedia): Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria formed 1 January 1914

Roman Empire.note: Hadrian gave up Trajan's conquests east of the Euphrates (Armenia, Mesopotamia, Assyria) in 117; Rome did not hold a province of Mesopotamia again until Septimius Severus in 198. Hadrian gave up Trajan's conquests beyond the Euphrates in 117. Later sacks of Ctesiphon (165, 198, 283) were raids and not conquests. The map no longer draws Babylonia as Roman in those years, and after Jovian's treaty of 363 it leaves out Nisibis and the lands east of the Tigris. Zenobia's Palmyrene empire held Syria and Egypt in 270–271, so they are left blank, and the Gallic Empire, retaken by Aurelian in 274, is shown as Roman from 275. In 198 Severus made Nisibis the capital of a Roman province of Mesopotamia, but the map still draws it outside the empire.

sources.title: Mesopotamia (Roman province) (Wikipedia): evacuated 117 by Hadrian, re-established by Severus in 198

Xin Dynasty.note: In 23 CE the Xin was collapsing: Han-restorationist rebels from Hubei beat Wang Mang's army at Kunyang and took Chang'an in October, so the gaps show land already lost to rebels; at its height the Xin held the full Han realm. Wang Mang proclaimed the Xin in 9 CE and it fell in 23 CE, so the map's Xin outlines for 6-8 and 24-29 CE are shown as Han: the Gengshi Emperor took Chang'an in 23, and Guangwu made Luoyang the Han capital in 25.

sources.title: Xin dynasty (Wikipedia): Battle of Kunyang (June-July 23), Chang'an captured October 23, Lülin rebels from Hubei

Western Jin.note: Eastern Jin (317-420), the southern successor state ruled from Jiankang after the Western Jin fell in 316. Liu Yu ended the Eastern Jin in 420 and founded the Liu Song. Before 316 the outline is trimmed east of 126°E: Gungnae (Ji'an), on the Yalu, was Goguryeo's capital from 3 to 427, while Jin's Lelang commandery around Pyongyang lasted until 313.

sources.title: Jin dynasty (266-420) (Wikipedia): Western Jin ended 316; Eastern Jin 317-420 at Jiankang
Goguryeo (Wikipedia): Gungnae 3-427, Pyongyang 427-668; Silla took the Han River valley 553; fell 668
Lelang Commandery (Wikipedia): 108 BC-313 AD, seat at modern Pyongyang, conquered by Goguryeo 313

Türgesh.note: Second Turkic Khaganate: in 692–704 this polygon over Mongolia shows the Eastern Türks under Qapaghan Qaghan; the Türgesh khaganate (from 699) lay farther west in Zhetysu, ruling from Suyab and Taraz. From 705 to 744 the eastern part of this shape, over Mongolia, is the Second Turkic Khaganate, centred on Ötüken in the Orkhon valley, and is shown under that name. The Türgesh, whose capitals were Suyab and Taraz, held the Chu and Talas valleys; their western lands are not drawn in these years. After the Uyghurs took Ötüken in 744 only the western part is shown as Türgesh.

sources.title: Second Turkic Khaganate (Wikipedia): 682–744, centred on Ötüken; Ötüken taken by the Uyghurs in 744

Uyghur Khaganate.note: After 766 the Karluks held Zhetysu (the Chu–Talas valleys around Suyab), so the western tip of this shape was outside Uyghur rule.

Dzungar Khanate.note: In November 1717 a Dzungar army seized Lhasa and occupied central Tibet until a Qing expedition expelled it in 1720; that occupation is not drawn here.

First Mexican Empire.note: Mexico's claimed border ran to 42°N and took in all of Alta California and New Mexico (today's California, Nevada, Utah and Arizona), though most of that interior was controlled by the Comanche, Apache, Ute and other peoples rather than by Mexico.

Samanid Empire.note: At this date Rayy and the Jibal belonged to the Buyids and Kerman to the effectively independent Ilyasids; Samanid rule in the south and west was nominal at best.

Argentine Confederation.note: Much of the Gran Chaco in the north remained under the control of Indigenous peoples such as the Qom and Wichí until military campaigns from the 1880s, so the Confederation's real reach was smaller than drawn. After the Battle of Pavón (1861) Buenos Aires rejoined and the country was reunited as the Argentine Republic in 1862; it is labelled so from 1862.

British East Africa.note: British colonies in Africa: this shape groups Britain's remaining African dependencies during decolonisation (1961–1968), not the East Africa Protectorate, which was the forerunner of Kenya from 1895 to 1920. From 1965 only the southern African dependencies (Bechuanaland and Basutoland to 1966, Swaziland to 1968, and Rhodesia, which declared independence in 1965) are drawn; Uganda (1962), Kenya (1963), Malawi and Zambia (1964) and the Gambia (1965) had become independent. In 1963–64 the map still draws Uganda and Kenya as British for a year or two too long.

Free French.note: In 1940 Chad was the first colony to join Free France (26 August), though the map leaves it out; Gabon joined only after fighting in November, and the Pacific colonies and French India also rallied that summer.

Emirate of Diriyah.note: At its height the first Saudi state held Najd, the Hejaz, al-Hasa and the Gulf coast, with Asir and Tihama as vassals; the Zaydi imams kept Sanaa and the Yemeni highlands, and the Rub' al Khali was not administered.

Kushan Empire.note: Kushan power in the Tarim Basin rested on influence in Kashgar, Yarkand and Khotan (coins, a client king in Kashgar); Kucha and Turfan in the northeast belonged to the Han-dominated Western Regions, not to the Kushans. From 91 to 237 the empire is drawn south of about 40.3°N, which removes the map's arm along the northern Tarim Basin (Kucha, Turfan), Han territory at the time.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Protectorate of the Western Regions

Median Kingdom.note: Later Greek tradition gives the Medes a realm from northeastern Iran to the Halys River in Anatolia, including Armenia and former Assyrian lands; the map's eastern reach to Bactria is speculative, and some historians doubt a large Median empire existed.

Estado Novo.note: Portugal's Estado Novo ended with the Carnation Revolution of April 1974; Cabinda has been part of Angola since independence in 1975. India annexed Goa, Daman and Diu in December 1961, but the map still shades Goa as Portuguese until 1974. Goa, Daman and Diu are not shown as Portuguese after India annexed them in December 1961.

Centralist Mexico.note: Centralist Mexico — the 1842–1845 'Federated Republic of Mexico' polygon (Nuevo México) was a department of the Centralist Republic, not a separate state.

Ghurid Dynasty.note: After Muhammad of Ghor died in 1206 the empire broke apart: Khwarazm took Herat and Ghor, Yildiz held Ghazni, and Qutb al-Din Aibak ruled the Indian conquests from Delhi; the map's 1206–1209 outline still shows the earlier unified realm.

Qin Dynasty.note: Qin Dynasty — the 'Minyue' polygon of 221–207 BCE (Jiangxi and inland Fujian) lay inside Qin commanderies; Minyue proper was in Fujian.

(Eighteen Kingdoms).note: Jiangxi belonged to the kingdom of Hengshan and northern Hunan to Linjiang; the area shown as Minyue here was not part of Minyue, which lay in Fujian.

Liao Dynasty.note: From 1115 the Jurchen Jin broke away in the northeast, taking Huanglong (1115) and everything east of the Liao River (1116) and the Supreme Capital in 1120, so the map overstates Liao after 1115; Liao also kept garrison towns far west on the Mongolian steppe.

Hotaki Dynasty.note: Ashraf Hotaki ruled central and southern Persia from Isfahan, while Khorasan was held by Tahmasp II and Nader and Herat by the Abdali Afghans; Hussain Hotaki ruled Kandahar. Nader expelled Ashraf from Persia in 1729 and took Kandahar in 1738. The Afghans took Isfahan in 1722 but never held Khorasan or the Caspian provinces; Nader drove Ashraf out of Isfahan in 1729, after which the Hotaki state is drawn only around Kandahar (taken by Nader in 1738).

Aq Qoyunlu.note: Until Uzun Hasan's victory over the Qara Qoyunlu in 1467, the Aq Qoyunlu held only Diyarbakır and nearby Upper Mesopotamia; Iraq and Khuzestan belonged to others. The Aq Qoyunlu never held Ankara (Ottoman throughout); that detached piece is removed. Ismail I took Tabriz in 1501 and defeated the last Aq Qoyunlu rulers by 1503, taking Baghdad in 1508; from 1504 their lands are shown as Safavid.

Nanda Empire.note: The Nandas ruled the Ganges plain from Magadha. The lands west of the Beas, including Punjab and Sindh, were separate kingdoms when Alexander arrived in 326–325 BCE. The Nanda frontier was the Beas, so the shading across Sindh is too far west.

sources.title: Nanda Empire (Wikipedia): Nanda territory lay beyond the Beas; Kalinga in part, Avanti probable, nothing south of the Vindhyas

Assyrian Egypt.note: Neo-Assyrian Empire (without Egypt); Egypt in 650–616 BCE belongs to the Twenty-sixth (Saite) Dynasty under Psamtik I This shape repeats the whole Assyrian empire together with Egypt. Psamtik I was in control of all Egypt by 654 BCE, so only its Egyptian part is kept, shown as the Twenty-sixth (Saite) Dynasty for 650–616 BCE; Assyria itself is drawn by the Neo-Assyrian Empire's own shape.

sources.title: Psamtik I (Wikipedia): unified all of Egypt under his rule by 656 BCE; firmly in control by 654 BCE

Neo-Assyrian Empire.note: Assyria conquered Egypt in 671 BCE but lost it within about 15 years. By 656 BCE Psamtik I, first installed as an Assyrian client, ruled a reunited Egypt on his own. From then on, Egypt shown as Assyrian means at most nominal allegiance. Babylon kept its own kings until Tiglath-Pileser III took it in 729 BCE, and Damascus fell in 732 BCE, so neither is drawn as Assyrian before then. Lake Van, the heart of Urartu with its capital Tushpa, was never Assyrian. Egypt, conquered in 671 BCE, was independent under Psamtik I by 654 BCE. Babylon rose under Nabopolassar in 626 BCE. Nineveh fell in 612 BCE and Harran in 610–609 BCE, and the former Assyrian heartland is shown as Babylonian from 611 BCE. Egypt held the Levant until the Battle of Carchemish in 605 BCE.

sources.title: Psamtik I (Wikipedia): unified all of Egypt by 656 BCE

Moghulistan.note: By 1517 Moghulistan had split. Sultan Said Khan founded the Yarkent Khanate at Kashgar in 1514 and Mansur Khan ruled from Turpan, while the Kyrgyz had driven the Moghuls out of the northern steppe by 1510–11.

sources.title: Moghulistan (Wikipedia): Kyrgyz drove out the Moghuls by 1510–11; Yarkent Khanate formed 1514; 1517 division of Yarkent and Turpan

Greco-Bactrian Kingdom.note: Demetrius I may have taken Arachosia from the Mauryas around 190–180 BCE ('Demetrias in Arachosia' is attributed to him), but this is uncertain. Some maps include Arachosia and others do not.

sources.title: Demetrius I of Bactria (Wikipedia): 'may have first started to recover' Arachosia; invasion of NW India 190–180 BCE

Pala Empire.note: Kings of Avanti, Madra and Gandhara are listed attending Dharmapala's court. They only recognised his overlordship and kept their own lands, so the Palas never governed Malwa or the Punjab. By the 820s the Pratiharas also held Kannauj.

sources.title: Pala Empire (Wikipedia): Avanti, Madra and Gandhara rulers 'maintained their own territories'; Nagabhata II took Kannauj

Mamluk Dynasty.note: In 1272, under Balban, Malwa was still ruled by the Paramara kings. Delhi first conquered it under Alauddin Khalji in 1305.

sources.title: Paramara dynasty (Wikipedia): Arjunavarman II ruled Malwa 1274–1285; Alauddin Khalji's forces took Malwa in 1305

Kara-Khanids.note: The khanate's eastern core was Kashgar, one of its capitals. In 1006 Yusuf Qadir Khan of Kashgar conquered the Buddhist kingdom of Khotan, so the Tarim basin's western half belonged to the khanate.

sources.title: Kara-Khanid Khanate (Wikipedia): capitals included Kashgar; Khotan conquered 1006

(First French Empire).note: In 1812 the Empire formally annexed only Catalonia, as four departments created on 26 January 1812. The rest of northern Spain was held by French armies but still belonged to Joseph Bonaparte's Kingdom of Spain, and the Russian lands were held only briefly during the 1812 invasion.

sources.title: Bouches-de-l'Èbre (Wikipedia): created 26 January 1812 on Catalonia's annexation by the French Empire

British Gold Coast.note: Lagos was governed from the Gold Coast from 1874 to 1886 and then became a separate colony, so the shapes in southern Nigeria are not part of the 1896 Gold Coast. The Gold Coast itself reached inland toward Ashanti, which was made a British protectorate in 1896. Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957, so from 1957 only the Nigerian part of this shape is drawn (Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960).

sources.title: Lagos Colony (Wikipedia): administered under the Gold Coast 1874–1886, separate colony from 1886

Shunga Empire.note: Kalinga regained its independence after the Mauryas fell and was ruled by its own Mahameghavahana kings, such as Kharavela, not by the Shungas. By the early 1st century BCE the Shungas held little beyond the central Ganges plain and Vidisha.

sources.title: Kharavela (Wikipedia): Kalinga regained independence after the Maurya Empire; Kharavela dated 2nd–1st century BCE

Mali Empire.note: By the 1430s Mali was in decline: it had lost Gao, and Timbuktu fell to the Tuareg in 1433, so the eastern Niger bend shown here was no longer Malian. From 1434 the map leaves Timbuktu, Gao and the eastern Niger bend outside Mali, in line with the loss of Timbuktu to the Tuareg in 1433–34.

Swedish Empire.note: The German area shows where Swedish armies held sway in the Thirty Years' War (1631–34); after Nördlingen it was lost, and in 1648 Sweden kept only Pomerania, Wismar and Bremen-Verden. Historians date Sweden's age as a great power ('the Swedish Empire') to 1611–1721; from 1722 the state is labelled the Kingdom of Sweden.

Kingdom of Great Britain.note: United Kingdom (from 1801; the Kingdom of Great Britain existed 1707–1800) The United Kingdom's shape no longer includes the Gulf states after 1971: Bahrain and Qatar became independent in August–September 1971 and the United Arab Emirates on 2 December 1971 (Oman was never a British colony). Before 1972 the map also keeps Kuwait (independent 1961), Cyprus (1960) and Aden (1967) inside the United Kingdom for a few years too long. The United Kingdom's shape is removed from South Yemen after independence (Nov 1967), Kuwait after 1961 and Cyprus after 1960; the British sovereign base areas on Cyprus (Akrotiri and Dhekelia) are too small to draw here.

First Spanish Republic.note: Kingdom of Spain (Bourbon Restoration from 29 December 1874)

British Cape Colony.note: This shape lumps other British possessions with the Cape: Natal and British Kaffraria were separate colonies, and the West African dots are Sierra Leone and the Gambia. Under the Peace of Amiens the Cape was handed back to the Batavian Republic in 1803 and held by it until the British reconquest of January 1806.

Gurjara-Pratihara Dynasty.note: At its height under Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala I (c. 836–910) the empire ruled from Kannauj and reached Bihar and the Bengal frontier, wider than shown here.

Yuezhi.note: Chinese sources place the Yuezhi between Dunhuang and the Qilian Mountains in Gansu; they reached the Ili valley only after the Xiongnu defeated them c. 176 BCE.

Khanate of Khiva.note: Outside the Khorezm oasis, the Turkmen and Kazakh nomads only loosely acknowledged Khiva, and from 1855 to 1867 the Turkmen were in open revolt.

Khazaria.note: The area south of the Caucasus marks the Khazar raid of the 760s into Albania, Iberia and Armenia; the lasting frontier with the Caliphate was at Derbent. The khaganate ended when Sviatoslav of Kiev sacked its capital Atil in about 965–969.

sources.title: Khazars (Wikipedia): khaganate c. 650–969; Atil capital until c. 965–969

(Mahajanapadas).note: Each patch marks only the core around a capital. The sixteen great states (mahajanapadas) were kingdoms and republics that covered much of the Ganges plain, Malwa and the northern Deccan.

French Indochina.note: Indochina was Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia and the leased port of Guangzhouwan; the far-off islands and Indian ports also shaded here (New Caledonia, Réunion, French India) were separate French colonies. The Indochinese Union was formed in 1887; before that France held Cochinchina (Saigon taken 1859, provinces ceded 1862 and 1867) and protectorates over Cambodia (1863) and Annam–Tonkin (1883–84). Laos and Cambodia became independent in 1953 and the Geneva Accords of July 1954 ended French Indochina.

Khanate of Bukhara.note: Khorasan and Herat, south of the Amu Darya, were fought over with Safavid Persia; the Uzbeks besieged Herat in 1527-28 but were beaten at Jam in 1528, so they did not firmly rule this area.

Indus Valley Civilization.note: Only a few major city sites are marked; the Harappan world spread across most of today's Pakistan and northwest India, from Baluchistan to Haryana and south to Gujarat.

Indo-Sasanian Empire.note: The Kushano-Sasanian lands are known mostly from coins and Persian inscriptions; besides Bactria and Gandhara they probably took in Sogdiana and the mint cities of Merv and Herat, so the frontiers here are approximate.

Marinid Sultanate.note: Abu Inan took Tlemcen (1352), Bejaia (1353) and briefly Tunis (1357), but he had to pull out of Ifriqiya in 1357 and died in 1358; by 1359 the Zayyanids and Hafsids had their lands back.

Kingdom of Germany.note: Otto I also took the separate crown of Italy (claimed 951, conquered 961, emperor 962); northern Italy, shaded here with Germany, stayed a distinct kingdom with the same ruler.

Gallic Empire.note: Spain also recognised Postumus as emperor from 260 until about 269, so the Gallic Empire briefly reached well beyond what is shaded here. Aurelian retook the Gallic Empire after the Battle of Châlons in 274, so its lands are shown as Roman from 275.

Zhou Dynasty.note: Early Zhou kings ruled the Wei and Yellow River valleys and planted fiefs such as Qi, Lu and Yan, but the eastern Shandong peninsula (Lai) and the Huai River lands stayed with independent Yi peoples.

Vakataka Kingdom.note: The Vakataka dynasty faded out after Harishena (died c. 500-510), so the kingdom is not shown after that.

Songhai Empire.note: At its height Songhai also held the Dendi lands down the Niger below Gao and the Saharan salt mines of Taghaza, and took tribute from Agadez and some Hausa cities, beyond what is shaded here. Songhai rule on the Niger bend ended with the Moroccan victory at Tondibi in March 1591, after which Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné were taken; the Askia dynasty survived downstream in Dendi, which is not shown.

Denmark-Norway.note: Greenland was also a Dano-Norwegian colony from 1721, held through trading and mission stations along its west coast; it is not shaded here. Denmark–Norway ended with the Treaty of Kiel in 1814, when Norway passed to Sweden; later years are labelled Denmark. Iceland became a separate kingdom in personal union with Denmark on 1 December 1918 and is not drawn as Danish after 1918.

Nanyue.note: Fujian and southern Zhejiang belonged to the separate Yue kingdoms of Minyue and Dong'ou; Zhao Tuo won their submission for a time, but Nanyue never governed them.

Chu.note: In the early 3rd century BCE Chu also held most of Hunan, south to the Nanling hills; Qin took its heartland at Ying in 278 BCE, and this map leaves the southern lands out. Chu's northern frontier ran along the Fangcheng hills; the map had drawn it over Xinzheng (capital of Zheng, then Han), Daliang (capital of Wei) and Shangqiu (capital of Song), so its outline is trimmed at about 34.15°N. After Qin took the Chu capital Ying in 278 BCE, the land west of about 112.5°E is no longer shown as Chu.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Chu (state) ("included most of the present-day provinces of Hubei and Hunan")
Qin's wars of unification (Wikipedia): Han 230, Zhao 228, Wei 225, Chu 223, Yan 222, Qi 221 BC

Kingdom of Pontus.note: By the 1st century CE the Roman client kingdom of Pontus was only the eastern half of the old kingdom; the west (Paphlagonia, Amaseia, Amisus) was part of Roman Galatia and Bithynia-Pontus. Nero annexed the rest in 62 CE.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pontus (region) ("larger part of Pontus ... included in the province of Galatia ... eastern half ... client kingdom")

(Kingdom of England).note: In 1700 England, Scotland and Ireland shared one monarch but were separate kingdoms; England and Scotland merged into Great Britain only in 1707.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Acts of Union 1707 ("had shared a monarch since the 'personal' Union of the Crowns in 1603")

Anti-Kuomintang Coalition.note: In mid-1930 the coalition of Yan Xishan, Feng Yuxiang and the Guangxi clique held most of North China (Shanxi, Hebei with Peiping, Henan, Shaanxi and Gansu) plus Guangxi, and set up a rival government in Peiping; this map shows far less.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Central Plains War (coalition held Henan, took Jinan in Shandong, held Guangxi, set up a government in Peiping)

Talpur Dynasty.note: The Talpur Mirs ruled Sindh (with Khairpur and Mirpur branches) and some border districts; Balochistan, Kalat and Makran were under their own khans. The Talpur Mirs ruled Sindh from Hyderabad, Khairpur and Mirpur Khas until the British conquest of 1843. Kalat and Balochistan were not theirs, and the map's polygon in the far north (Gilgit and Hunza, 1840–1894) belongs to other states, so only Sindh is drawn.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Talpur dynasty (combined area "over 100,000 square kilometres")

Maukhari Dynasty.note: The Maukharis of Kannauj ruled the Ganges plain from about Thanesar to Magadha; Bengal (Gauda) was a rival kingdom that later took Maukhari land.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Maukhari dynasty ("spread from Thaneshwar in the West to Nalanda district in the east")

Indo-Parthians.note: At its height under Gondophares, the Indo-Parthian kingdom also held its homeland of Sistan (Drangiana) and Arachosia in what is now south-western Afghanistan, besides Gandhara, Sindh and western Punjab.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Indo-Parthian Kingdom (Gondophares originally ruled Seistan; held Arachosia, Sindh and Punjab; Taxila a capital)

Yadava Dynasty.note: The Seuna Yadavas ruled the western Deccan from Devagiri; their raids into Tripuri and Bhandara in the east were short-lived, and the Raichur doab changed hands with the Kakatiyas. The Yadava (Seuna) kingdom ended in 1317 and Devagiri became a province of the Delhi Sultanate, so the 1318–1325 outline is shown as Delhi territory. Malwa, north of the Narmada, belonged to the Paramaras, not the Yadavas, and is not drawn as Yadava land.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Seuna (Yadava) dynasty (Ramachandra occupied Tripuri, subdued Bhandara; lost Raichur to the Kakatiyas)

Weimar Republic.note: The Weimar Republic ended in 1933 when the Nazis took power; from then on Germany is the Third Reich. Northern Schleswig voted to join Denmark in 1920 and was transferred on 15 June 1920; it is no longer drawn as German.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Weimar Republic ("from 9 November 1918 to 23 March 1933")

Khanate of Kokand.note: When Shahrukh Biy founded the Kokand Khanate in 1709 it held only part of the Fergana Valley; Tashkent was conquered about a century later, and Samarkand stayed Bukharan.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Khanate of Kokand (Tashkent conquered under Alim Khan, r. 1799-1811; Samarkand held only about six months)

Bahmani Sultanate.note: In 1390 the Bahmani Sultanate held the western and central Deccan; Warangal and eastern Telangana were conquered in the 1420s, and the Konkan coast later still.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bahmani Sultanate (Ahmad Shah I, r. 1422-1436, "finally captured the remnants of Warangal")

Rustamid dynasty.note: The Rustamid imams at Tahert ruled central and western Algeria; Ibadi communities in Jebel Nafusa, Fezzan and oases such as Ouargla recognised them, but the Sahara was not under direct rule.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rustamid dynasty (authority "over what is now central and western Algeria"; recognized by the Ibadis of Wargla, Jebel Nafusa, Fezzan)

Minyue.note: Minyue lay in what is now Fujian, east of the Wuyi Mountains; Jiangxi to the west was Han's Yuzhang commandery. In 221–207 BCE the polygon labelled Minyue (Jiangxi and inland Fujian) lay inside Qin commanderies and is shown as Qin; Minyue proper was in Fujian.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Minyue ("an ancient kingdom in what is now the Fujian province")

North German Confederation.note: In late 1870 German armies occupied much of northern France during the Franco-Prussian War; this was a wartime occupation, not part of the North German Confederation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: North German Confederation (map shows Alsace-Lorraine, annexed after the 1870-71 war, separately from the Confederation)
German Confederation — Wikipedia (members incl. Austria, Bavaria; Province of Prussia and Posen only included 1848–1851)

Sarbadars.note: In 1345 the Sarbadars held only the area around their capital Sabzevar in western Khorasan (roughly Semnan to Nishapur); the Caspian coast, Gorgan and the Rey district shown here belonged to Togha Temür and other rulers.

sources.title: Sarbadars — Wikipedia (after 1344 most conquests lost; Gurgan was Togha Temür's capital; Ray gained only after 1353)

Ostrogoths.note: After Odoacer's defeat in 493 the Ostrogothic kingdom held the whole Italian peninsula and Sicily, which are missing from this outline; Provence and Sirmium were added only in 504–508.

sources.title: Ostrogothic Kingdom — Wikipedia (after 493 'masters of Italy'; Sirmium 504–505; Provence from 508)

Panthay Rebellion.note: The Panthay (Dali) sultanate was based in western Yunnan and fought across Yunnan province; it never held Sichuan, which this outline wrongly includes.

sources.title: Panthay Rebellion — Wikipedia (uprisings across Yunnan; Dali the centre; Sichuan 'not in rebellion')
Zimbabwe Rhodesia — Wikipedia (1 June 1979 – 18 April 1980; became Republic of Zimbabwe)

Emirate of Bukhara.note: Around 1800 the emirate was centred on Bukhara and Samarkand between the Amu Darya and the Zarafshan; the eastern hill states (Hisor, Kulob, Karategin, Darvaz) and the Pamirs shown here were only added between the 1820s and the late 19th century.

sources.title: Emirate of Bukhara — Wikipedia (core between Amu and Syr Darya; begliks expanded under Nasrullah 1827–1860; Darvaz c.1878; Pamirs late 19th c.)

Malaysia.note: From September 1963 to August 1965 Singapore was a state of Malaysia; the island is not shaded here for those years. Singapore left Malaysia on 9 August 1965; the map shows it inside Malaysia until 1966.

sources.title: Singapore in Malaysia — Wikipedia (state of Malaysia 16 September 1963 – 9 August 1965)

Kingdom of Prussia.note: From 1815 to 1867 most of Prussia's territory is drawn under the German Confederation label; the small area shown here is Neuchâtel, a Swiss principality ruled by the Prussian king. Northern Bohemia is not drawn as Prussian in 1757-1761: Frederick II's army was in Bohemia only from April to July 1757, and the province stayed Austrian.

sources.title: German Confederation — Wikipedia (Prussia a member state; Confederation included Austria, Bavaria and others)
New Netherland — Wikipedia (1614–1667 and 1673–1674; Delmarva to Cape Cod; Dutch Brazil a separate colony)

Himyarite Kingdom.note: In the 1st century BCE Himyar was a young highland kingdom around Zafar in south-west Yemen. It did not rule the Red Sea coast north into the Hejaz, and it took Saba only around 25 BCE and Hadramawt around 300 CE. Aksum conquered Himyar about 525; Abraha then ruled Yemen as an Aksumite viceroy, and from about 570 Yemen was under Sasanian Persia.

Sultanate of Muscat and Oman.note: The Qatar peninsula drawn here was never part of Muscat and Oman: from 1916 it was a separate British protectorate under the Al Thani. From 1920 the interior around Nizwa was ruled by the autonomous Imamate of Oman.

sources.title: History of Qatar (Wikipedia): 1916 Anglo-Qatari treaty made Qatar a British protectorate

Southern Han.note: Northern Vietnam (Jinghai, or Annam) was ruled by local Vietnamese governors, not Southern Han. Southern Han held it only briefly around 930–931, and its 938 invasion was defeated at the Bach Dang River.

South African Republic.note: The detached block east of Swaziland is Tongaland (Maputaland), a Tsonga kingdom the Transvaal never ruled; Britain annexed it in 1895.

sources.title: Maputaland (Wikipedia): Tongaland annexed by Great Britain on 11 June 1895
History of Qatar (Wikipedia): British protectorate 1916–1971 on the Qatar peninsula

Late Pallava Empire.note: In the 4th century the Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram over the northern Tamil country and southern Andhra; the far south around Madurai was under the Kalabhras. The 'Later Pallava' kingdom began with Simhavishnu around 575.

Kingdom of Khotan.note: Khotan ruled the oases of the southern rim of the Tarim Basin. Kashgar and the northern oases such as Aksu belonged to the Kara-Khanids and the Uyghurs; Khotan held Kashgar only briefly after 970.

Nguyễn dynasty.note: From 1834 to 1841 Emperor Minh Mạng annexed most of Cambodia as the province of Trấn Tây (not shown here), until Siamese-backed revolts forced a withdrawal.

sources.title: Confederation of the Rhine (Wikipedia): excluded Austria, Prussia, Danish Holstein and Swedish Pomerania; area 325,700 km²

Heian Japan.note: Shikoku was part of the Heian state but is missing from this outline; in 1183–85 it was a Taira stronghold, site of the Battle of Yashima. Northern Honshu (Mutsu and Dewa) was ruled autonomously by the Northern Fujiwara in the 12th century.

sources.title: Battle of Yashima (Wikipedia): Taira fortress at Yashima, Sanuki Province, Shikoku

Ghana Empire.note: By around 1200 Ghana's former vassals (Sosso, Diara, Mali and others) had grown stronger than the old core, and the Sosso conquered the capital by 1203, so this outline overstates the late kingdom.

Netherlands Antilles.note: Surinam (Dutch colony); hide from 1976, when the Republic of Suriname polygon takes over

sources.title: Netherlands Antilles (Wikipedia): existed 1954–2010; Suriname was a separate colony

Republic of Liberia.note: In 1848 the new republic governed only a coastal strip of settler towns; the interior shown here was claimed later, and Maryland (Cape Palmas) joined only in 1857.

Sayyid Dynasty.note: The Sayyids also claimed Punjab (Lahore, Dipalpur, Multan) until Multan broke away under the Langahs in the late 1430s, though Khokhar chiefs contested it; the map shows only the Delhi core.

Empire of Haiti.note: Divided Haiti: northern State and southern Republic Haiti was an empire only under Dessalines (1804–06) and Soulouque (1849–59); from 1820 to 1849 and after 1859 it was a republic and is labelled so.

relabel.name: Haiti (divided: northern State and southern Republic)
relabel.key: Haiti (divided: northern State and southern Republic)

British Overseas Territories.note: There are 14 British Overseas Territories; this map draws only the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, Bermuda and Gibraltar, leaving out the Caribbean territories, St Helena, Pitcairn, the Indian Ocean Territory and the Cyprus bases.

Russian-occupied territories.note: Russian forces have held Transnistria since 1992; Abkhazia and South Ossetia are counted as occupied from 2008, Crimea from 2014, and parts of eastern and southern Ukraine from 2014 and 2022. This outline does not change over time, wrongly includes Moldova's Gagauzia, and leaves out Abkhazia, Crimea and occupied Ukraine.

Sultanate of Zanzibar.note: The Sultanate (Unguja and Pemba only; Mafia Island had passed to Germany in 1890) was overthrown on 12 January 1964 and Zanzibar joined Tanganyika that April.

Danish India.note: Tranquebar on the Coromandel coast, Danish from 1620 to 1845 and the capital of Danish India, is missing from the map before 1800.

Federated Republic of Mexico.note: In 1842–1845 the separate polygon here (Nuevo México) was a department of the Centralist Republic and is shown as part of it. In 1836–1841 too, the northern polygon (New Mexico and the north) was part of the Centralist Republic, not a separate federal state.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Santa Fe de Nuevo México

Maurya Empire.note: The data's polygon reaches the far south, but Ashoka's own Rock Edicts II and XIII name the Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras and Keralaputras as peoples beyond his frontier; the southernmost Ashokan inscriptions (Maski, Brahmagiri, Siddapur) lie around 14–15°N. The empire is drawn north of about 13.8°N. The map never shows the lands Seleucus I ceded around 303 BCE (the Kabul valley and Arachosia around Kandahar), although Ashoka's Greek and Aramaic edicts at Kandahar show Maurya rule there. After Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last Maurya king c. 185 BCE, the remaining outline (184-171 BCE) is shown as the Shunga Empire. Gedrosia (Makran), west of the lower Indus, came to the Maurya only with Seleucus' cession, so before 303 BCE it is cut out of the empire.

sources.title: Wikimedia Commons: Maurya Empire, c.250 BCE (map)

Kingdom of Lunda.note: This shape, between the Atlantic, the lower Congo and the Kwango around Mbanza Kongo (São Salvador), is the Kingdom of Kongo, reunited in 1709 after its civil war and a Portuguese vassal from 1857; after the Berlin Conference the lower Congo north of the river mouth went to the Congo Free State. The Lunda Empire lay far to the east, around its royal capital (musumba) near the upper Kasai, and is not drawn on the map.

Mali Federation.note: The Mali Federation of Senegal and French Sudan broke up when Senegal withdrew on 20 August 1960; from September 1960 this shape is the Republic of Mali.

Burkina Faso.note: The country was the Republic of Upper Volta until it was renamed Burkina Faso in 1984.

Republic of Benin.note: Independent in 1960 as the Republic of Dahomey; the country took the name Benin in 1975.

Tanzania.note: Tanganyika became independent on 9 December 1961 and united with Zanzibar to form Tanzania on 26 April 1964.

Belgian Congo.note: Until 1908 this was the Congo Free State, owned personally by King Leopold II; Belgium annexed it as the Belgian Congo in 1908. After the Congo became independent on 30 June 1960, the remaining piece is Ruanda-Urundi, a Belgian-run trust territory until Rwanda and Burundi became independent on 1 July 1962.

Zululand.note: After the Anglo-Zulu War of 1879 the kingdom was broken up, and Britain annexed Zululand in 1887; it was joined to Natal in 1897.

Kamerun.note: German traders were active at Douala from 1868, but Germany declared its Kamerun protectorate only in 1884; before that the Duala kings ruled the estuary.

Kingdom of Axum.note: Aksumite rule in Yemen ended when the Persians took Sana'a in 570, so Yemen is not shaded as Aksumite after that.

Danish Gold Coast.note: Denmark sold Christiansborg and its other Gold Coast forts to Britain in 1850.

Massina Empire.note: Ségou, the Bambara capital, was never part of Massina; the Ségou kingdom lasted until Umar Tall took it in 1861.

Sokoto Caliphate.note: Bornu, under al-Kanemi, drove the Fulani out after they sacked its capital in 1808, so the lands west and south-west of Lake Chad around Kukawa (Bornu's new seat from 1814) were never part of the Caliphate.

Republic of Colombia.note: Under the 1863 constitution the country was the United States of Colombia until the 1886 constitution made it the Republic of Colombia; it is labelled so for 1866–85.

Republic of Baja California.note: William Walker declared this republic at La Paz in November 1853 and abandoned it in May 1854, so the 1855 shape is shown as Mexico. The 1856 shape is Nicaragua, where Walker made himself president in July 1856.

Republic of the Rio Grande.note: This federalist revolt ended with Antonio Canales's surrender at Camargo on 6 November 1840; the 1841 shape is shown as Mexico.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Republic of the Rio Grande

California Republic.note: The Bear Flag republic lasted only from 14 June to 9 July 1846, when US forces took over; the 1847 shape is shown as Mexican territory, which in law it stayed until the 1848 treaty.

France Antarctique.note: The French colony on Guanabara Bay (1555–67) was driven out by the Portuguese, who founded Rio de Janeiro in 1565 and won in January 1567; the 1567–71 shape is shown as Portuguese. The small shape in Florida is Fort Caroline, a separate French colony destroyed by Spain in 1565, and is not drawn after that.

Itza Mayans.note: Spanish forces took Nojpetén, the Itza capital, in March 1697; the 1697–99 shape is shown as Spanish.

Saint Kitts.note: This shape is Saint Croix in the US Virgin Islands (bought from Denmark in 1917), not Saint Kitts, so it is shown as part of the United States. Saint Kitts and Nevis, independent since 1983, is not drawn on this map.

Antigua and Barbuda.note: Antigua was a self-governing British associated state from 1967 and became independent on 1 November 1981; before that it is shown as British.

Saint Vincent.note: Saint Vincent was a British associated state from 1969 and became independent on 27 October 1979; before that it is shown as British.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines

Kingdom of Hawaï'i.note: The monarchy was overthrown in January 1893; a provisional government ruled until the Republic of Hawaii was proclaimed on 4 July 1894.

French Louisiana.note: Louisiana was handed back to France in 1800 but Spain ran it until 30 November 1803, and France passed it to the United States on 20 December 1803. This shape also holds France's Caribbean islands and Guiana, so it is labelled French colonies in the Americas; Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804.

Los Altos.note: Los Altos broke away as a sixth Central American state in 1838 and was reconquered by Rafael Carrera in January 1840; the 1841 shape is shown as Guatemala.

New France.note: Louisiana passed to Spain (agreed in 1762–63, with Spanish rule firm from 1769), so from 1769 the shape no longer covers it. Quebec fell in September 1759 and Montreal in September 1760, but the map keeps Canada French until the Treaty of Paris in 1763.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Battle of the Plains of Abraham

Toltec.note: Tula, the Toltec capital, lies just west of the shape drawn here.

Norse Greenland.note: Norse settlers arrived around 985. The Western Settlement was abandoned around 1360; the Eastern Settlement around Brattahlíð and Hvalsey, which lies east of the shape drawn here, lasted longer: its last written record is a wedding in 1408.

Empire of Brazil.note: Brazilian troops occupied Asunción after the Paraguayan War until 1876, but Paraguay remained a separate state; the map shades it as Brazilian in 1870–76.

Bolivia.note: Chile occupied Bolivia's coast, including Antofagasta, in 1879 and kept it under the 1884 truce; Bolivia ceded it by the 1904 treaty, when the map moves it to Chile.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Treaty of Peace and Friendship (1904)

Chimu Empire.note: The Inca conquered Chimor around 1470; the map keeps it independent until 1481.

Qi.note: Qi surrendered to Qin in 221 BCE, completing the unification, so in 221-219 BCE its land is shown as Qin.

sources.title: Qin's wars of unification (Wikipedia): Han 230, Zhao 228, Wei 225, Chu 223, Yan 222, Qi 221 BC

Wei.note: The outline labelled Wei in the Warring States lay in central and northern Hebei, which belonged to Zhao (and, until Zhao annexed it in 296 BCE, to the small state of Zhongshan around Lingshou); it is shown as Zhao, trimmed south of Yan's capital Ji. Wei itself held southern Shanxi and the lands around its capital Daliang (Kaifeng), which the map does not draw.

sources.title: Wei (state) (Wikipedia): capitals Anyi, then Daliang (Kaifeng) from 361 BC; surrendered to Qin 225 BC
Zhao (state) (Wikipedia): capital Handan; Hebei and Shanxi; conquered Zhongshan; Dai remnant to 222 BC
Zhongshan (state) (Wikipedia): capital Lingshou (Pingshan, Hebei); annexed by Zhao 296 BC

Zhongshan.note: The outline labelled Zhongshan lies around Ji (Beijing), the capital of Yan, so it is shown as Yan; Zhongshan itself lay further south-west around Lingshou until Zhao annexed it in 296 BCE.

sources.title: Yan (state) (Wikipedia): capital Ji (Beijing); Ji fell 226 BC, Yan overrun 222 BC
Zhongshan (state) (Wikipedia): capital Lingshou (Pingshan, Hebei); annexed by Zhao 296 BC

Later Zhou.note: Before 256 BCE this small outline is the royal domain of the Eastern Zhou kings, extinguished by Qin in 256 BCE; the Later Zhou dynasty (951-960) gave way to the Song in February 960.

sources.title: Zhou dynasty (Wikipedia): capital moved east 771 BC; royal domain extinguished by Qin 256 BC
Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (Wikipedia): Later Liang 907-923, Jin at Taiyuan, Later Tang 923, Later Jin 936-947, Later Han 947-951, Later Zhou 951-960
Song dynasty (Wikipedia): Kaifeng 960-1127; Jingkang 1127; Lin'an (Hangzhou); Lin'an fell 4 Feb 1276; Yamen 1279

Later Han.note: The Later Han ended in 951, when Guo Wei founded the Later Zhou; Taiyuan and central Shanxi then became the separate Northern Han, which this outline does not split off.

sources.title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (Wikipedia): Later Liang 907-923, Jin at Taiyuan, Later Tang 923, Later Jin 936-947, Later Han 947-951, Later Zhou 951-960

Later Jin.note: In 911-921 this outline is the Jin state of Li Keyong and Li Cunxu, based at Taiyuan, not the Later Jin dynasty of 936-947.

sources.title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (Wikipedia): Later Liang 907-923, Jin at Taiyuan, Later Tang 923, Later Jin 936-947, Later Han 947-951, Later Zhou 951-960

Former Jin.note: Li Cunxu proclaimed the Later Tang in 923 and conquered the Later Liang the same year.

sources.title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (Wikipedia): Later Liang 907-923, Jin at Taiyuan, Later Tang 923, Later Jin 936-947, Later Han 947-951, Later Zhou 951-960

Later Liang Dynasty.note: The Later Liang fell to the Later Tang in 923.

sources.title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (Wikipedia): Later Liang 907-923, Jin at Taiyuan, Later Tang 923, Later Jin 936-947, Later Han 947-951, Later Zhou 951-960

Cao Cao.note: Cao Cao died in 220 and his son Cao Pi founded the state of Wei the same year, with its capital at Luoyang.

sources.title: Three Kingdoms (Wikipedia): Wei 220 (Luoyang), Shu 221 (Chengdu), Wu at Jianye; Shu fell 263, Jin 266, Wu fell 280

Eastern Wu.note: Wu's capital Jianye fell to the Jin in 280, ending the Three Kingdoms.

sources.title: Three Kingdoms (Wikipedia): Wei 220 (Luoyang), Shu 221 (Chengdu), Wu at Jianye; Shu fell 263, Jin 266, Wu fell 280
Jin dynasty (266-420) (Wikipedia): Luoyang sacked 311, Chang'an taken 316; Eastern Jin at Jiankang 317-420; Liu Song 420

Southern Qi.note: The Southern Qi gave way to the Liang in 502.

sources.title: Northern and Southern dynasties (Wikipedia): Liu Song 420-479, Qi 479-502, Liang 502-557, Chen 557-589 at Jiankang

Liang Dynasty.note: Chen Baxian ended the Liang at Jiankang in 557 and founded the Chen.

sources.title: Northern and Southern dynasties (Wikipedia): Liu Song 420-479, Qi 479-502, Liang 502-557, Chen 557-589 at Jiankang

Chen Dynasty.note: Sui troops took Jiankang in 589 and the last Chen emperor surrendered.

sources.title: Sui dynasty (Wikipedia): founded 581 at Chang'an; took Jiankang 589; Luoyang from 605; ended 618

Northern Zhou.note: Yang Jian took the Northern Zhou throne in March 581 and renamed the state Sui.

sources.title: Northern Zhou (Wikipedia): capital Chang'an; founded 557; took Northern Qi 577; replaced by Sui 581
Sui dynasty (Wikipedia): founded 581 at Chang'an; took Jiankang 589; Luoyang from 605; ended 618

Western Wei.note: The Northern Zhou replaced the Western Wei at Chang'an in 557.

sources.title: Northern Zhou (Wikipedia): capital Chang'an; founded 557; took Northern Qi 577; replaced by Sui 581

Eastern Wei.note: Gao Yang deposed the last Eastern Wei emperor in 550 and founded the Northern Qi at Ye.

sources.title: Eastern Wei (Wikipedia): capital Ye 534-550; replaced by Northern Qi in 550

Northern Song.note: The Jurchen Jin took Kaifeng in January 1127 and the Song court moved south (the Southern Song, later at Lin'an, modern Hangzhou). From 1130 the north (Henan, Shandong and Shaanxi) was held by the Jin and their client state, so the Song outline is trimmed north of about 33.5°N.

sources.title: Song dynasty (Wikipedia): Kaifeng 960-1127; Jingkang 1127; Lin'an (Hangzhou); Lin'an fell 4 Feb 1276; Yamen 1279
Jin dynasty (1115-1234) (Wikipedia): took Kaifeng Jan 1127; Zhongdu 1153-1214; Kaifeng 1214-1233; fell 1234

Southern Song.note: Yuan forces captured the capital Lin'an (Hangzhou) on 4 February 1276; Song loyalists fought on in the south until the Battle of Yamen in 1279, so in 1276-78 Lin'an and the lands north of it are no longer shown as Song.

sources.title: Song dynasty (Wikipedia): Kaifeng 960-1127; Jingkang 1127; Lin'an (Hangzhou); Lin'an fell 4 Feb 1276; Yamen 1279

Taebong.note: In 918 Gung Ye of Taebong was overthrown and Wang Geon founded Goryeo.

sources.title: Taebong (Wikipedia): Gung Ye overthrown and Wang Geon installed in 918
Goryeo (Wikipedia): founded 918 at Kaesong; Silla annexed 935; Tamna incorporated 1105; ended 1392

Goryeo.note: Goryeo ended in July 1392, when Yi Seong-gye founded Joseon.

sources.title: Goryeo (Wikipedia): founded 918 at Kaesong; Silla annexed 935; Tamna incorporated 1105; ended 1392
Joseon (Wikipedia): founded 1392; capital Hanseong; Korean Empire proclaimed 1897

Tamna.note: Tamna (Jeju) was formally annexed by Goryeo in 1105; from 1275 to 1301 it was a Yuan prefecture.

sources.title: Tamna (Wikipedia): officially annexed by Goryeo 1105; Yuan Tamna Prefecture 1275-1301

Gojoseon.note: Wiman Joseon fell to the Han in 108 BCE; its lands became Han commanderies, among them Lelang with its seat at Pyongyang.

sources.title: Wiman Joseon (Wikipedia): destroyed by Han c. 108 BC; Four Commanderies set up
Lelang Commandery (Wikipedia): 108 BC-313 AD, seat at modern Pyongyang, conquered by Goguryeo 313

Byeonhan.note: The last Gaya state, Daegaya, fell to Silla in 562.

sources.title: Gaya confederacy (Wikipedia): Geumgwan Gaya fell to Silla 532, Daegaya 562

Kenmu Restoration.note: The Kenmu Restoration lasted 1333-1336; Ashikaga Takauji took Kyoto in 1336 and founded the Ashikaga shogunate, while Go-Daigo's Southern Court held out at Yoshino.

sources.title: Kenmu Restoration (Wikipedia): 1333-1336; Ashikaga Takauji entered Kyoto Feb 1336
Ashikaga shogunate (Wikipedia): 1336-1573, seat Kyoto; ended when Nobunaga drove out Yoshiaki

Northern Fujiwara.note: Minamoto no Yoritomo destroyed the Northern Fujiwara and took Hiraizumi in 1189.

sources.title: Northern Fujiwara (Wikipedia): seat Hiraizumi; destroyed by Yoritomo in 1189

Tokugawa Shogunate.note: The Ryukyu Kingdom (Okinawa and the islands south of it, capital Shuri) was never part of the shogunate: Satsuma made it a vassal in 1609, but it kept its king and its tribute ties with China until Japan annexed it in 1872-79, so it is not shown as Tokugawa (the map has no outline of its own for it). Satsuma annexed the Amami islands in 1611. The shogunate ended with the Meiji Restoration of January 1868; in 1868-69 the outline still covers the lands fought over in the Boshin War.

sources.title: Ryukyu Kingdom (Wikipedia): Okinawa united 1429, capital Shuri; Satsuma vassal from 1609 but de jure independent; Okinawa Prefecture 1879
Tokugawa shogunate (Wikipedia): 1603-1868, governed from Edo; ended 1868

Kuomintang.note: This outline covers nearly all of China; until 1928 its internationally recognised government was the Beiyang government in Beijing, while the Kuomintang ran a rival government in Guangzhou from 1917. The Nationalists, based at Nanjing from 1927, unified the country in 1928. It is shown as the Republic of China.

sources.title: Beiyang government (Wikipedia): internationally recognised government of the ROC at Beijing, 1912-1928; rival Guangzhou government from 1917
Nationalist government (Wikipedia): capital Nanjing from 1927; wartime retreat to Chongqing

Great Mongol State.note: The Mongolian People's Republic was proclaimed on 26 November 1924; from 1919 to 1921 Mongolia was occupied by Chinese troops.

sources.title: Bogd Khanate of Mongolia (Wikipedia): 1911-1919 and 1921-1924, capital Niislel Khuree; MPR proclaimed 26 Nov 1924

Communist Party of China.note: The Red Army abandoned the Jiangxi Soviet and its capital Ruijin in October 1934, at the start of the Long March.

sources.title: Jiangxi Soviet (Wikipedia): 1931-1934, capital Ruijin; abandoned October 1934

relabel.name: Kingdoms of England, Scotland and Ireland
Kingdoms of England, Scotland and Ireland

Kingdom of England.note: Paris returned to the French in April 1436, so English rule around Paris and in Burgundian lands is no longer drawn for 1436–39 (Paris shows no state there for those years). Normandy fell in 1449–50 and Gascony in 1451–53; they are no longer drawn as English from 1451 (Bordeaux was briefly English again in 1452–53). Calais was taken by France in January 1558; the Pale of Calais is no longer drawn as English from 1558 (the town shows no state until the map's French outline reaches it in 1579). From 1603 England, Scotland and Ireland shared one king (the Union of the Crowns) but stayed separate kingdoms until the 1707 Acts of Union; where the map draws them as one shape it is labelled 'Kingdoms of England, Scotland and Ireland', and as the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1708. The map does not show Rouen as English between its capture in January 1419 and its loss in October 1449.

Viking settlements.note: Norse Dublin fell to the Anglo-Normans in 1170, and Norway ceded the Hebrides to Scotland by the Treaty of Perth in 1266; Dublin is not drawn as a Viking settlement after 1170, and the Hebrides not after 1266.

Almoravid Dynasty.note: Aragon took Zaragoza in December 1118, so the city is no longer drawn as Almoravid in 1119–29. The Almohads took Marrakesh and the Almoravids lost their empire in 1147; from 1148 only the Almoravid remnant in the Balearic Islands is drawn. The Almohads took Marrakesh in 1147, ending Almoravid rule in Morocco; after that only Almoravid remnants in al-Andalus and the Balearic Islands are drawn.

Taifa of Valencia.note: James I of Aragon took Valencia in October 1238; from 1239 the former taifa is shown as part of the Crown of Aragon (the Muslim south around Xàtiva held out until the mid-1240s).

Novgorod Republic.note: Ivan III of Moscow annexed Novgorod in 1478; the map's 1478–81 Novgorod shape is shown as the Grand Principality of Moscow.

Pskov Republic.note: Pskov was annexed by Moscow in 1510; its 1510–11 shape is shown as the Grand Principality of Moscow.

Habsburg Monarchy.note: In the Third Partition (1795) Warsaw went to Prussia, not Austria; the map's Habsburg outline wrongly reached Warsaw and western Mazovia in 1794–1805 and that area is removed.

Austrian Empire.note: Warsaw was Prussian until 1806 and then part of the Duchy of Warsaw; the Austrian outline that wrongly reached Warsaw in 1806–10 is removed there. Kraków joined the Duchy of Warsaw in 1809 but is still drawn Austrian in 1810.

French Fourth Republic.note: The French sector of Berlin lay in the north-west of the city; the map's French outline covered all of Berlin, including East Berlin, and is removed there. The French occupation zone of 1945–49 is also drawn too far north (Bonn was in the British zone).

French Fifth Republic.note: Algeria became independent in July 1962, the Comoros in 1975 and Djibouti in 1977, but the map's outline for France kept them until 2023, and also kept a French Berlin sector until 1990. These areas are removed from France after independence; Mayotte and the overseas departments remain French.

New Caledonia.note: Before 1860 this outline bundles several French colonies (New Caledonia, Réunion), so it is labelled French colonies. Its 1859 shape over all of Cochinchina is removed: France took Saigon in February 1859, but the provinces were ceded only in 1862 and 1867.

First Hellenic Republic.note: The First Hellenic Republic ended in 1832, when Greece became a kingdom; the state is shown as the Kingdom of Greece (1832–1923 and 1936–40) and the Second Hellenic Republic (1924–35).

Principality of Bulgaria.note: Bulgaria declared independence and became a tsardom (kingdom) on 5 October 1908; from 1908 it is labelled the Kingdom of Bulgaria.

United Principalities of Moldavia and Wa.note: Romania became a kingdom in 1881; from 1881 the state is labelled the Kingdom of Romania. In 1917–18 the map draws all of Romania under Austria-Hungary, though Iași and Moldavia stayed Romanian.

sources.title: United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia (Wikipedia)

Serbs.note: This outline is the Serbian state, not a people: Revolutionary Serbia (1804–13), the Principality of Serbia (1815–81) and, from 1882, the Kingdom of Serbia.

Serbian Empire.note: The Serbian Empire broke up in 1371; its core is shown as Moravian Serbia (1371–1402) and the Serbian Despotate (1402–1459). The Ottoman occupation of 1439–44 is not drawn.

Hungarian Republic.note: Hungary was restored as a kingdom (with a regent, Miklós Horthy) in 1920 and remained one until 1946; 1920–43 is labelled the Kingdom of Hungary. The map keeps Cluj in Romania in 1940–44, though the Second Vienna Award gave northern Transylvania to Hungary, and draws Košice under Germany though it was Hungarian from 1938.

Kingdom of Lithuania.note: The Kingdom of Lithuania lasted only a few months in 1918; interwar Lithuania was a republic with Kaunas as its temporary capital. Grodno, Polish from 1921, is no longer drawn inside Lithuania.

Free City of Danzig.note: The Memel Territory was under Allied administration from 1920 and annexed by Lithuania in 1923; it was never part of the Free City of Danzig and is no longer drawn with it.

Principality of Monaco.note: Monaco is a city-state of about 2 km²; the map's shapes for it were far too large and lay over Nice, so they are trimmed to Monaco itself, which is too small to show at most zooms.

Kingdom of Monaco.note: Monaco has never been a kingdom: it is the Principality of Monaco. Its shapes for 1815–1939 lay over Nice and are trimmed to Monaco itself.

County of Ribagorza.note: Before 1085 this shape lies around Pamplona, not Ribagorza (a small Pyrenean county far to the east); it is the Kingdom of Pamplona, later called Navarre.

County of Foix.note: In 1482–1511 this shape includes Pamplona and Upper Navarre, an independent kingdom ruled by the Foix and Albret families; it is labelled the Kingdom of Navarre. Castile conquered Upper Navarre in 1512.

Duchy of Burgundy.note: After Charles the Bold died in January 1477, Louis XI of France seized the Duchy of Burgundy; from 1478 only the Burgundian Netherlands are drawn under this name.

Kingdom of Gwynedd.note: Edward I completed the conquest of Gwynedd in 1283; its 1283–84 shape is shown as England.

sources.title: Conquest of Wales by Edward I (Wikipedia)

Latin Empire.note: The Empire of Nicaea retook Constantinople on 25 July 1261, ending the Latin Empire; it is not drawn after 1260. The Empire of Nicaea retook Constantinople on 25 July 1261, restoring the Byzantine Empire; from 1262 the city is shown with the Nicaean (restored Byzantine) state, not the Latin Empire.

Visigothic Kingdom.note: The Umayyads invaded in 711, defeated King Roderic and took Toledo; the 712–717 shape covering the peninsula is shown as Umayyad. (Visigothic Septimania, around Narbonne, held out until about 720.)

sources.title: Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula (Wikipedia)

Grand Duchy of Berg.note: The Grand Duchy of Berg was a small Napoleonic state on the lower Rhine (1806–13). The large 1814 shape under its name is France after Napoleon's first abdication and is shown as the Bourbon Kingdom of France.

Crown of Castile.note: Granada surrendered on 2 January 1492; the city itself is no longer drawn as Castilian in 1487–91.

Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.note: Trieste was never part of Yugoslavia: it was under Allied military government from 1945, the Zone A of the Free Territory of Trieste from 1947, and Italian from 1954. The city is no longer drawn as Yugoslav.

Yugoslavia.note: Fiume (Rijeka) was annexed by Italy in 1924, while neighbouring Sušak stayed Yugoslav; the city west of the Rječina is no longer drawn as Yugoslav in 1924–40.

Austria-Hungary.note: In 1918 Romania kept Moldavia and its wartime capital Iași, and Bessarabia joined Romania in April 1918; they are no longer drawn as Austro-Hungarian.

Brandenburg-Prussia.note: Stettin and the mouth of the Oder were Swedish from 1648 until the 1720 Treaty of Stockholm; they are no longer drawn as Brandenburg's.

Republic of Genoa.note: Genoa ceded Corsica to France in May 1768 and France conquered the island in 1769; Corsica is no longer drawn as Genoese from 1769.

Kingdom of Jerusalem.note: Acre fell to the Mamluks on 18 May 1291 and the last crusader towns on the coast were given up that summer; from 1291 the remnant is shown as Mamluk.

County of Tripoli.note: The Mamluk sultan Qalawun took Tripoli in April 1289, ending the county; from 1289 its land is shown as Mamluk.

Principality of Antioch.note: Baybars took Antioch in May 1268, ending the principality; from 1268 its land is shown as Mamluk.

Kingdom of Israel.note: Assyria took Samaria in about 722–720 BCE and made the kingdom an Assyrian province; from 720 BCE its land is shown as Assyrian.

Philistia.note: Philistia was the coastal plain of the Philistine cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath); before 1000 BCE the map drew it over the hill country, Jerusalem and Galilee, so it is now limited to the coast.

Hyksos.note: The Hyksos (Fifteenth Dynasty) ruled northern Egypt from Avaris from about 1650 BCE until Ahmose expelled them about 1550 BCE; the realm is shown only in those years.

Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt.note: The Saite dynasty ruled Egypt from 664 BCE until the Persian king Cambyses II won at Pelusium in 525 BCE.
