Regency of Algiers.note: Algiers surrendered to the French on 5 July 1830, ending the regency. From 1831 only the French-held coast is drawn; the Beylik of Constantine (to 1837) and the Emir Abd al-Qadir's state in the west are not shown.

Zayyanid dynasty.note: From 1516–1517 Algiers and the land east of Tenes belonged to the Barbarossa brothers and then the Ottoman regency of Algiers; the Zayyanids kept only the Tlemcen region until the Ottomans took it in the 1550s.

Hafsid Dynasty.note: Spain took Bejaia and Tripoli in 1510 (Tripoli passed to the Knights of Malta in 1530 and to the Ottomans in 1551), so from 1511 the Hafsid kingdom is drawn without them.

Wattasid dynasty.note: The Saadians took Marrakesh in 1524–1525 and from 1527 held southern Morocco; the Wattasids kept only the kingdom of Fez in the north until 1554.

Germiyanids.note: The Germiyanid beylik was the Kütahya region of western Anatolia; the map had attached to it detached areas around Ankara (Ottoman from the 1350s), in Upper Mesopotamia and at Derbent, which are removed.

Hashemite Arab Federation.note: This polygon is southern Iraq, which the Jalayirid sultans held from Wasit and Basra after losing Baghdad in 1410 until the Qara Qoyunlu took it in 1432; it is shown under those names (the Hashemite Arab Federation was a 1958 union of Iraq and Jordan).

Mahdids.note: This polygon is Oman, ruled by the Nabhani dynasty (about 1154–1624) whose capital was in the interior; its 1475–1506 coastal remnant around Muscat and Qalhat was a dependency of the Kingdom of Ormus. The Mahdids were a Yemeni dynasty of Zabid (1159–1173).

Nabhani Dynasty.note: This polygon is Yemen: the Mahdids of Zabid ruled the Tihama from 1159 until the Ayyubid conquest of 1173–1174. The Nabhani dynasty ruled Oman.

Najahid Dynasty.note: The Mahdids took Zabid from the Najahids in 1159.

Ziyadid dynasty.note: Ziyadid rule at Zabid ended in the early 11th century; from 1022 Zabid was ruled by the Najahids, so later polygons are shown under that name.

Hamdanid Emirates.note: The Hamdanid dynasty ended in 1004. Later polygons under this name were patchworks of other local powers (the Mirdasids of Aleppo, Uqaylids of Mosul, Marwanids of Diyarbakir, and later Anatolian, Afghan and Gulf principalities) and are shown simply as regional emirates.

Arab Federation.note: The Arab Federation of Iraq and Jordan lasted from February to July 1958; after the 14 July revolution Iraq was a republic, so in 1959 the Iraqi part is shown as the Iraqi Republic (Jordan is not drawn that year).

United Arab Republic.note: Syria left the union on 28 September 1961; Egypt kept the name United Arab Republic until 1971, so from 1961 it is drawn without Syria.

State of Israel.note: From 1948 to 1967 the Gaza Strip was held by Egypt, not Israel, so the map's Israel of those years is drawn without it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: United Arab Republic occupation of the Gaza Strip

Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd.note: Ibn Saud merged his kingdoms as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia on 23 September 1932.

Emirate of Nejd.note: After the battle of Mulayda (1891) the Rashidi emirs of Ha'il ruled Riyadh and Najd until Ibn Saud retook Riyadh in January 1902.

Pahlavi Dynasty.note: Reza Khan was prime minister from 1923, but the Qajar dynasty was deposed only on 31 October 1925 and he was proclaimed shah in December 1925.

Kingdom of Armenia.note: The Arsacid kingdom of Armenia ended in 428, when Persia replaced its king with a governor (marzban); later polygons are shown as Sasanian Armenia.

Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party.note: This is Syria under Ba'ath rule (the Syrian Arab Republic), shown as a state rather than a party.

Ghaznavid Empire.note: The Ghaznavids lost their last stronghold, Lahore, to the Ghurids in 1186, so the realm is not shown after that. Their Punjab frontier lay west of Delhi, which the Tomara kings ruled until about 1152 and the Chahamanas after them; the map's eastern spur over Delhi and Haryana (1044–1176) is not drawn.

Chauhan Dynasty.note: After the Second Battle of Tarain (1192) the Chahamana kingdom of Ajmer passed to the Ghurids; Hariraja's revolt ended in 1194, so the 1195–1201 outline is shown as Ghurid territory.

Sena Dynasty.note: The Ghurid general Bakhtiyar Khalji took Nadia and Lakhnauti (Gaur) around 1205. The later Sena kings held only eastern Bengal from Bikrampur until about 1230.

Bijapur Sultanate.note: After Talikota (1565) Bijapur took the Raichur Doab, but Penukonda was the Vijayanagara capital until 1592 and the lands south of the Tungabhadra stayed with the Aravidu kings, so they are not drawn as Bijapur's before 1619.

Ahmadnagar Sultanate.note: The Ahmadnagar Sultanate ended in 1636, when the Mughals and Bijapur partitioned it; Daulatabad fell to the Mughals in 1633.

Berar Sultanate.note: Berar was annexed by the Ahmadnagar Sultanate in 1574 and ceded to the Mughals in 1596.

Durrani Empire.note: The Durranis held the Kashmir valley until 1819, but never Ladakh, which was an independent Namgyal kingdom until the Dogra conquest of 1834; the Sikhs took Sirhind and the eastern Punjab from 1764. Those lands are not drawn as Durrani after 1763.

Emirate of Afghanistan.note: Dost Mohammad's emirate ruled from Kabul; Kashmir was Sikh from 1819 and Ladakh was conquered by the Dogras in 1834, so the map's eastward extension over Gilgit, Baltistan and Ladakh (1828–39) is not drawn.

Satavahana Dynasty.note: Kalinga (coastal Odisha) was a separate kingdom under Kharavela's Mahameghavahana dynasty, a rival of the Satavahanas, so it is not drawn as Satavahana land.

Mahameghavahana Dynasty.note: Kharavela ruled Kalinga; his campaigns against Magadha, the Satavahanas and the Tamil kings were raids, not lasting conquests, so only Kalinga is drawn. His dates are uncertain (2nd or 1st century BCE).

Islamic Republic of Pakistan.note: East Pakistan became independent Bangladesh on 16 December 1971, so it is not drawn as part of Pakistan in 1972.

Sind-Habbari Dynasty.note: Mahmud of Ghazni ended Habbari rule in Sindh in 1026; from then the Soomra dynasty ruled Sindh, and the later outline is shown under its name.

Ayutthaya Kingdom.note: Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese in April 1767. Siamese armies besieged Pegu in 1595 and reached it in 1600 but never held it; Siam's gains in Burma were the Tenasserim coast and, for a time, the Mon country around Martaban.

Sukhothai Kingdom.note: Sukhothai was a vassal of Ayutthaya from 1378 and was annexed in 1438.

Kingdom of Mrauk U.note: Arakan (Mrauk U) was conquered by Burma's Konbaung dynasty at the start of 1785.

Konbaung Dynasty.note: Before 1757 the Lower Burma kingdom based at Pegu was the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom (1740–1757), which took Ava in 1752; Alaungpaya's Konbaung dynasty, founded at Shwebo in 1752, conquered Pegu in May 1757.

First Toungoo Empire.note: The First Toungoo Empire collapsed in 1599; the Nyaungyan or Restored Toungoo dynasty ruled from Ava until Hanthawaddy forces took the city in 1752. The northern kingdom shown from 1752 is Alaungpaya's new Konbaung dynasty at Shwebo.

Trưng sisters.note: The Trưng sisters rose against Han rule in 40 CE and were defeated by Ma Yuan in 43 CE; the map shows them only in 43.

Đại Việt.note: Under this name the map shows the Mạc dynasty (1527–1592) and its remnant in Cao Bằng (to 1677). The small southern territory shown from 1653 is Panduranga, the last Cham principality, a Vietnamese vassal from the 1690s until Minh Mạng annexed it in 1832.

Tây Sơn dynasty.note: The Trịnh army took Phú Xuân (Huế) in 1774–75 and held it until Nguyễn Huệ's northern campaign of 1786.

Kingdom of Cambodia.note: From the coup of March 1970 until Phnom Penh fell to the Khmer Rouge on 17 April 1975 Cambodia was the Khmer Republic; the monarchy was restored in September 1993.

People's Republic of Kampuchea.note: The People's Republic of Kampuchea (1979) was renamed the State of Cambodia in 1989 and gave way to the restored Kingdom of Cambodia in September 1993.

Sultanate of Brunei.note: Brunei at its height ruled the coasts of northwest Borneo and had influence in Sulu and around Manila Bay, but it never ruled Mindanao; Spain took Manila in 1571.

Rajahnate of Cebu.note: Legazpi's expedition took Cebu in 1565, making it the first Spanish capital in the Philippines.

Sultanate of Banten.note: Jayakarta was a Banten dependency until the Dutch razed it and founded Batavia on its site in 1619.

Sultan of Yogyakarta.note: The Yogyakarta Sultanate was created by the Treaty of Giyanti in 1755, when Mataram was split in two.

Surakarta Sunanate.note: Surakarta became a separate realm with the Treaty of Giyanti in 1755; before that it was Mataram's capital (from 1745).

Sultanate of Aceh.note: The Dutch took Aceh's capital, Kutaraja (Banda Aceh), in January 1874 and the last sultan surrendered in 1903, though guerrilla resistance went on for years. After 1945 Aceh was Republican territory and then a part of Indonesia, not a restored sultanate.

Sultanate of Kedah.note: Siam transferred Kedah to Britain by the Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 10 March 1909.

Republic of Indonesia.note: Western New Guinea stayed Dutch after 1949 and passed to Indonesia only in 1963 (under UN administration from October 1962). East Timor, occupied from 1975, came under UN administration in 1999 and became independent on 20 May 2002; the map still shows it as Indonesian until 2005. East Timor is not shown as Indonesian after the 1999 referendum; it became independent in 2002 (the small Oecusse exclave is too small to separate here).

Blue Horde.note: Tokhtamysh took Sarai in 1380 and reunited the Horde's two wings, so from 1380 this shape is shown as the Golden Horde (the duplicate copy drawn over the Golden Horde in 1385–1401 is hidden). Its later polygon in Crimea is shown as the Golden Horde until 1441 and then as the Crimean Khanate, founded that year by Hacı I Giray.

sources.title: Blue Horde (Wikipedia): Tokhtamysh united the Blue Horde with the White Horde in 1380
Tokhtamysh (Wikipedia): khan of the Golden Horde 1380–1395
Crimean Khanate (Wikipedia): established by Hacı I Giray, 1441–1783

White Horde.note: From 1380, when Tokhtamysh of the White Horde took Sarai and reunited the Horde, this shape is shown as part of the Golden Horde.

Astrakhan Khanate.note: Russia took Astrakhan in 1556 and the khanate ended. The 1642–1768 polygon between the Don and the Volga continues the Don Cossacks' shape exactly and is the land of the Don Cossack Host, so it is shown under that name.

sources.title: Astrakhan Khanate (Wikipedia): Russia occupied Astrakhan in 1556
Don Cossacks (Wikipedia): the Don Cossack Host, independent or autonomous from the late 16th century to 1918

Turks.note: From 699 the former Western Turkic lands in Zhetysu were ruled by the Türgesh khaganate and are shown under that name.

sources.title: Türgesh (Wikipedia): established a khaganate in 699 after the demise of the Western Turks

Kazakh Khanate.note: Before 1505 the Kazakhs held the steppe and the towns of northern Turkestan; Samarkand, Bukhara and Tashkent were ruled by Timurids, Moghuls and then the Shaybanids, so the part of this shape south of the Syr Darya towns is left out for 1490–1504. Tawakkul Khan's capture of Samarkand in 1598 was short-lived.

sources.title: Kazakh Khanate (Wikipedia): c. 1495–96 division with Muhammad Shaybani; 1598 campaign
Khanate of Bukhara (Wikipedia): Shaybani conquered Samarkand, Bukhara, Tashkent and Andijan 1500–1503

Khwarezmid Empire.note: The Mongols took Otrar, Bukhara and Samarkand in 1220 and Gurganj and Merv in April 1221. From 1221 the Khwarazmian state is shown only in western Iran, where Jalal al-Din ruled from Tabriz from 1225 until he was killed in 1231, when it ended.

sources.title: Jalal al-Din Mangburni (Wikipedia): Tabriz 1225; killed 15 August 1231

Kingdom of Georgia.note: The united kingdom broke up into Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti in the late 15th century. The polygon around Tbilisi from 1468 is the Kingdom of Kartli, and from 1763 the united Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti, which Russia annexed in 1801.

sources.title: Kingdom of Kartli (Wikipedia): from the 1478 division until 1762, capital Tbilisi
Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti (Wikipedia): created 1762; annexed by Russia in 1801
Kingdom of Kakheti (Wikipedia): 1466–1762, capitals Gremi and Telavi

Great Yuan.note: 'Great Yuan' is a literal rendering of Dayuan, the Chinese name for the kingdom of the Ferghana valley (capital Ershi or Guishan, near Khujand), which the Han fought from 104 BCE. It has nothing to do with the later Mongol Yuan dynasty.

Akkadian Empire.note: The Akkadian Empire lasted from about 2334 to 2154 BCE; the map no longer draws it into the Gutian period (2153–2101 BCE). Sargon's first conquests (c. 2334–2300 BCE) are shown only from 2300 BCE, and Akkadian rule in Syria and Elam was patchy, resting on garrisons such as Susa and Tell Brak.

Babylonia.note: Hammurabi's kingdom at his death (1750 BCE) reached from Mari to the Gulf but not Assur. His son Samsu-iluna lost Ur and Uruk in the 1740s and Nippur by about 1720 BCE to the Sealand kings, so from then until 1595 BCE only northern Babylonia is drawn. In the 1300s Assur, independent from about 1363 BCE, is left out. Babylon was ruled from Assyria for long stretches. It is missing for 630–616 BCE, though Nabopolassar became king of Babylon in 626 BCE. After the Battle of Carchemish in 605 BCE it took the Assyrian west, and the map shows these western conquests only from 600 BCE.

sources.title: Wikimedia Commons: Hammurabi's Babylonia 1.svg (Babylonia in 1792 and 1750 BC)

Hittites.note: The Hittite capital Hattusa was abandoned and destroyed around 1190 BCE, and the empire is not drawn after 1180 BCE. Suppiluliuma I took northern Syria (Aleppo and then Carchemish) in the mid-1300s BCE, but the map shows Syria as Hittite only from 1300 BCE.

New Kingdom of Egypt.note: The New Kingdom ended with Ramesses XI's death in 1077 BCE. Later polygons are shown as the Twenty-first Dynasty (to 944 BCE) and the Twenty-second Dynasty (from 943 BCE). Thutmose III's conquest of Canaan (Megiddo, 1457 BCE) appears on the map only from 1400 BCE.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Third Intermediate Period of Egypt
Wikipedia: Battle of Megiddo (15th century BC)

Assyria.note: Middle Assyrian kings fought up to the Euphrates and took tribute beyond it. Carchemish and the land west of the river stayed Hittite, and after about 1180 BCE they formed a Neo-Hittite kingdom, so the map no longer draws Assyria west of the Euphrates.

Neo-Babylonian Empire.note: Cyrus took Babylon in October 539 BCE. From 538 BCE the map shows the empire's lands as Achaemenid Persian. The map leaves out Nabonidus's oasis holdings in Arabia (Tayma).

Achaemenid Empire.note: Persia lost Thrace and its other European lands after Plataea in 479 BCE, and Egypt broke away in 404 BCE. Both are left out of the empire in those years. Egypt was retaken in 343 BCE. Alexander took Babylon, Susa and Persepolis in 331–330 BCE, and Darius III died in 330 BCE, so from 330 BCE the lands still shown as Persian are drawn as Alexander's empire. The map dates Cyrus's eastern conquests (c. 545–539 BCE) to 550 BCE.

Gutian Dynasty.note: The map's only polygon for this name (2100–2001 BCE) covers Sumer, Akkad and Susiana in the years of the Third Dynasty of Ur, which had ended Gutian rule by about 2112 BCE; it is shown as the Third Dynasty of Ur.

sources.title: Wikimedia Commons: Map of Ur III.svg

Roman Kingdom.note: Rome's last king was expelled in 509 BCE, the traditional start of the Republic, so the city is shown as the Roman Republic from 509 BCE.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Overthrow of the Roman monarchy

Thirtieth Dynasty of Egypt.note: Artaxerxes III reconquered Egypt in 343 BCE (the Thirty-first Dynasty, a Persian satrapy), so Egypt in 342–338 BCE is shown as Achaemenid.

Sumerian City-States.note: Sumerian City-States is a collective name for many rival cities. Around 2500–2300 BCE the shape also takes in Mari on the middle Euphrates, which had its own kings. From 2100 BCE this name stands for the Third Dynasty of Ur, whose realm (Sumer, Akkad and Susa) is shown under that name. It collapsed by about 2004 BCE.

sources.title: Wikimedia Commons: Map of Ur III.svg

Macedonian Empire.note: After Alexander died in 323 BCE, his generals governed the provinces as satraps in the names of the kings Philip III and Alexander IV. The map shows this as one Macedonian Empire until about 308 BCE. In practice Ptolemy (Egypt), Antigonus (Asia) and, from 311 BCE, Seleucus (Babylon) acted independently.

Roman Republic.note: Before 481 BCE the Republic's own shape on the map does not cover the city of Rome, so the old kingdom's shape stands in for it from 509 BCE. Early Roman territory (a few hundred to a few thousand km²) is uncertain.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Overthrow of the Roman monarchy

Gupta Empire.note: Samudragupta's southern campaign (c. 350) defeated the kings of the east coast and the Pallava ruler of Kanchi, and frontier kingdoms paid tribute, but these lands were not annexed. From 347 the empire is drawn only between 18°N and 30.5°N, and east of 73°E until the conquest of the Western Satraps (c. 410, after which Saurashtra is kept), which removes Kanchi, Andhra, Punjab, Kashmir, Gandhara and most of the Indus valley; reference maps show Punjab and the Indus lands as tributary states.

sources.title: Wikimedia Commons: Map for Gupta Empire and tributaries

Lodi Dynasty.note: The Lodi dynasty ended when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat on 21 April 1526 and took Delhi and Agra; the map's Lodi outline for 1527-28 is hidden (the Mughal outline starts in 1529).

Mughal Empire.note: Humayun lost Punjab to Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and was in exile until 1545, so the 1541-46 outline is hidden. Kandahar was Safavid in 1622-38 and from 1649 (then Hotaki and, from 1738, Nader Shah's), so the empire is drawn east of 66.2°E in those years; from 1752 the Punjab (Lahore, Sirhind) was held by Ahmad Shah Durrani, so the 1752-61 outline is drawn east of 76.6°E. From 1762 the outline is cut to the Delhi region (Sirhind stayed with the Afghans and then the Sikhs), and after the British took Delhi in 1803 to the city itself: Rajput states such as Jaipur and Jodhpur were not under Mughal rule. Golconda, conquered in 1687, is missing from the map until 1700, and Raigad, Pune and Satara are cut out of the empire while the Marathas held them (1674-88 and 1708-29). Company forces captured Bahadur Shah II, the last emperor, on 20 September 1857, so the map ends the empire in 1857.

Southern Ming.note: Nanjing fell in June 1645, Fuzhou in 1646, and Guangzhou and Guilin in 1650; the Southern Ming outline is trimmed to match, which leaves some of this land blank. Taiwan under Koxinga's heirs (1662-83) is labelled the Kingdom of Tungning, and the anti-Qing lands of 1673-81 the Revolt of the Three Feudatories.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Revolt of the Three Feudatories

Later Jin Dynasty.note: Hong Taiji renamed the Later Jin the Qing in 1636, so the map labels it Qing from 1636. The Liaoxi corridor between Shanhaiguan and Jinzhou, which the Ming held until 1642 (Jinzhou) and 1644 (Ningyuan, Shanhaiguan), is cut out of the outline until then.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transition from Ming to Qing

Empire of Japan.note: Okinawa and the southern Ryukyus were annexed only in 1879, so before then the empire is drawn east of 128.5°E. Japan never ruled Fujian; the map's 1920-23 outline there is cut, though a thin coastal strip remains. Liaodong (Port Arthur), handed back to China in late 1895, and Qingdao, returned in 1922 and reoccupied in 1938, are cut out of the empire for 1896-97 and 1923-37. Singapore, Java and Rangoon, taken in early 1942, appear only from 1943. By the Treaty of Saint Petersburg (May 1875) Japan gave its part of Sakhalin to Russia in exchange for the northern Kuril Islands, so Sakhalin is cut out of the empire for 1875-76 (the map moves it to Russia only in 1877 and shows the northern Kurils as Japanese from 1877).

Qin.note: Qin conquered Chu in 223 BCE, but the map leaves Chu's southern lands around Changsha (Hunan) blank until 210 BCE.

Tughlaq Dynasty.note: Warangal, taken in 1323, was a Tughlaq province until the 1330s, and Madurai was ruled by the Madurai Sultanate from 1335 until the Vijayanagara conquest of 1378; the map shows neither.

Byzantine Empire.note: Constantinople fell to the Ottomans on 29 May 1453; from 1454 the map shows only the Despotate of the Morea, ruled by the last emperor's brothers until the Ottoman conquest in May 1460. Between 1204 and 1261 the empire's heir was the Empire of Nicaea, so no Byzantine Empire is drawn then. The map's data loses Thessalonica (1387) and Gallipoli (1354) years late, and wrongly shows Constantinople as Ottoman in 1402–1406.

Nicaean Empire.note: Nicaea recaptured Constantinople on 25 July 1261 and Michael VIII restored the Byzantine Empire; from 1261 the realm is labelled Byzantine.

Huns.note: The Huns' great raid of 395 through Armenia, Cappadocia and Syria was a campaign, not a conquest; the map no longer draws it as Hunnic territory.

Rashidun Caliphate.note: Hasan ibn Ali renounced the caliphate to Mu'awiya in August 661; from 662 these lands are labelled Umayyad.

Umayyad Caliphate.note: The Umayyads were defeated near Poitiers in October 732 and retreated over the Pyrenees, keeping only Septimania; Aquitaine is no longer drawn as Umayyad. After the Abbasid revolution of 750, al-Andalus was ruled by Yusuf al-Fihri until Abd al-Rahman I founded the Emirate of Córdoba in 756.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Fihri

Great Seljuk Empire.note: The Great Seljuk sultanate ended when Toghrul III was killed near Rayy on 19 March 1194; later polygons are hidden. The Fatimids took Jerusalem from its Seljuk-appointed governors in August 1098.

Timurid Empire.note: Timur's raids on the Golden Horde (1395), Syria (1400–01) and Ottoman Anatolia (1402) are no longer drawn as Timurid territory. The Qara Qoyunlu took Isfahan, Shiraz and Yazd from the Timurids in 1452–53, so western Iran is left undrawn from 1453. After 1507 the realm is Babur's Timurid principality of Kabul; his conquests in India from 1526 are labelled Mughal.

sources.title: Wikimedia Commons: Empire of Timur and his Campaigns

Safavid Dynasty.note: Isfahan fell to the Afghans in 1722; from 1723 only Tahmasp II's northern lands are drawn as Safavid. The map draws the Safavid conquest of the Aq Qoyunlu lands (1501–1508) several years late.

Kingdom of the Franks.note: From Pepin the Short's coronation in 751 the Frankish kingdom is the Carolingian realm, so it is grouped with the Carolingian Empire.

(Holy Roman Empire).note: The map's data stops grouping member states with the Empire after 1458; Bavaria, Saxony, Brandenburg, Trier, Bohemia and the Habsburg lands are regrouped here, but the Habsburg Monarchy's Austrian and Bohemian lands after 1515–1528 and Prussian Brandenburg after 1618 are still not highlighted, although they stayed in the Empire until 1806.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire
Wikimedia Commons: Map of the Holy Roman Empire, 1789

Tenochtitlan.note: The Mexica city-state is drawn as a small shape south-east of its true site on the western side of Lake Texcoco (about 19.43°N, 99.13°W); the island city itself falls inside the shape labelled Texcoco until 1428.

Kingdom of Portugal.note: Muscat, held by Portugal since 1507, surrendered to the Omani imam's forces on 23 January 1650; from 1650 it is no longer drawn as Portuguese.

Spanish Empire.note: Chile is left out from 1818, when it declared independence after the patriot victories of 1817–18 (the royalist south around Valdivia and Chiloé is also dropped for 1818–19). From 1826, when Callao and Chiloé, the last royalist strongholds, surrendered, no Spanish shapes are drawn in South America; the map had kept small Spanish pockets at Lima, La Paz, Carmen de Patagones and the Falklands until 1852. The map still shades Santo Domingo as Spanish after Spain withdrew in 1865, until 1872, and keeps northern Taiwan (Keelung and Tamsui) Spanish until 1658, although the Dutch expelled the Spanish garrison in 1642. Spain's colony in northern Taiwan (1626–1642) ended with the surrender of San Salvador (Keelung) to the Dutch in 1642, so Taiwan is not shown as Spanish afterwards.

Kingdom of Spain.note: Under the Treaty of Paris (December 1898) Spain gave up Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, so from 1899 only Spain's African territories are drawn with it. Between 1735 and 1761 the map still shades Naples and Sicily as Spanish, although they formed a separate kingdom under a junior Bourbon line from 1735; from 1762 they are drawn as the Kingdom of Naples and left out of Spain, as is the Duchy of Parma.

Francoist Spain.note: Equatorial Guinea (Spanish Guinea) became independent on 12 October 1968 and is not drawn as Spanish afterwards.

Batavian Republic.note: From June 1806 to July 1810 the Netherlands were the Kingdom of Holland under Louis Bonaparte, a French client state, before annexation to the French Empire.

Italian Republic.note: The Italian Republic became the Kingdom of Italy, with Napoleon as king, on 17 March 1805; it lasted until April 1814. Venetia (from 1806) and the Marche (from 1808) belonged to this kingdom, not to the French Empire, although the map draws Venice inside the Empire in 1809–10.

Helvetic Republic.note: Napoleon's Act of Mediation of 1803 replaced the Helvetic Republic with a restored Swiss Confederation of 19 cantons under French protection; it is shown under that name from 1803.

Kingdom of Naples (Napoleonic).note: Before 1806 this shape is the Bourbon Kingdom of Naples, shown under that name. The Napoleonic kingdom (Joseph Bonaparte from 1806, Murat from 1808) never held Sicily, where the Bourbon king ruled from Palermo under British protection until 1815, so Sicily is left out in 1806–14.

First French Empire.note: The map's shapes for these years spread over lands that were occupied, not annexed: Prussia after Tilsit (1807–08) stayed a kingdom, Spain and Portugal were Joseph Bonaparte's kingdom and a war zone, and the 1812 advance into Russia was reversed by December. These are left out; only Catalonia was formally annexed (1812).

German Empire.note: The Empire ended with the revolution of November 1918 and the Kaiser's abdication; the 1919 shape is the new German republic and no longer includes Courland. In 1915–18 the map draws German-occupied Belgium, Poland and the Baltic lands, and in 1918 Ukraine, as part of the Empire; they were occupied or client territories, not annexed.

Russian Republic.note: The Russian Republic proclaimed in September 1917 ended when the Bolsheviks seized power in November 1917 and dissolved the Constituent Assembly in January 1918. In 1918–19 Russia was split by civil war: the map leaves the Bolshevik-held centre around Moscow blank and shades the rest, held by White governments, Allied interventions and local authorities, as 'Russia (Civil War)'.

Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.note: Several shapes overreach: Tuva was a separate people's republic until it was annexed in October 1944; in 1945–52 the map draws Poland, and in 1945–48 Soviet-occupied eastern Germany, Austria, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and northern Korea and Manchuria, inside the USSR; Czechoslovakia is drawn inside it in 1969–90 because Soviet troops were stationed there after 1968; and in 1979–89 much of Afghanistan is drawn as Soviet during the war. None of these lands were part of the Union.

British Colonial Empire.note: Territories are removed from this shape once independent or transferred: Newfoundland and Labrador (joined Canada 1949), Fiji (1970), the Solomon Islands (1978), Belize (1981), the Bahamas (1973, removed from 1982) and Hong Kong (returned to China on 1 July 1997). Brunei (1984), Grenada (1974), Dominica (1978) and St Lucia (1979) remain drawn until 1995. The map also keeps Malaya and Singapore British during the Japanese occupation of 1942–45 (Singapore fell on 15 February 1942) and shades the British-occupied part of Iran in 1942–45 as British. Brunei is not shown as British after independence (1984); Malaya, Singapore, British Borneo, Burma and Hong Kong are not shown as British during the Japanese occupation (1942–1945).

sources.title: Transfer of sovereignty over Hong Kong — Wikipedia

Dutch Gold Coast.note: The shape on the coast of present-day Nigeria (Lagos and Badagry) drawn with the Dutch Gold Coast in 1861–72 was the British Lagos Colony, annexed in August 1861; it is removed.

Dutch East Indies.note: Small shapes that the map attached to the Dutch East Indies in India (one of them over Calcutta, 1809–45) and on the Danish-held Nicobar Islands are removed; the Dutch post in Bengal was at Chinsurah, north of Calcutta, until 1825.

Portuguese Empire.note: Eastern Hispaniola (Santo Domingo) and St Martin, drawn as Portuguese in 1805–14, were never Portuguese and are removed. The map also still shades Guadeloupe and Martinique as Portuguese in 1805–10 and French Guiana from 1805, although Portugal occupied French Guiana only from January 1809 to 1817.

Aztec Triple Alliance.note: Tlaxcala, east of the Valley of Mexico, was an independent enclave surrounded by the empire, never conquered, and became Cortés's chief ally; the map draws it inside the empire.

Kalabhra Dynasty.note: The Kalabhras are known mainly from hostile Pandya and Pallava records written centuries later, so both their dates and their extent are uncertain. Their rule probably began in the 3rd or 4th century (the map starts it only in 353), and Upinder Singh notes that 4th-century Pallava charters show they did not then rule near the Penner and Vellar rivers, so the northern edge drawn here, just south of Kanchipuram, is doubtful. Their rule ended in the last quarter of the 6th century: the Pallava Simhavishnu (c. 575–600) conquered the country up to the Kaveri and the Pandya Kadungon (c. 590–620; some date him c. 560–590) revived the Pandya kingdom south of it. The map's 592–601 remnant north of the Kaveri is therefore shown as Pallava; Kongu in the west, which the Western Gangas took in the mid-6th century, is left out.

-10000.why: The Okhotsk culture dates to c. 500–1000 CE and the Austronesian expansion from Taiwan began c. 3000 BCE; neither belongs to 10,000 BCE.

-8000.why: The Bantu expansion began c. 1500 BCE (the label covered most of Africa in 8000 BCE); Okhotsk and Austronesian labels are millennia too early.

-5000.why: Anachronisms for c. 5500–4500 BCE: Hurrians are attested from c. 2300 BCE, Elam from c. 3200 BCE, the Ainu culture from c. 1200 CE, Norte Chico from c. 3500 BCE, Funnelbeaker from c. 4300 BCE, Naqada I from c. 4000 BCE, Ghassulian from c. 4400 BCE; 'Dravidians' and 'Bantu' are language labels, not dated cultures.

-4000.why: For c. 4500–3500 BCE: Egypt unified c. 3100 BCE, Proto-Elamite c. 3200 BCE, Mature Harappan c. 2600 BCE, Kerma c. 2500 BCE, Minoan and Cycladic c. 3200–3100 BCE; Ur was not yet a state; 'Semites', 'Dravidians' and 'Bantu' are language labels. The archaeological cultures layer shows what is known for these centuries.
